2.	Yes. Contract provides for wage adjustments, holidays with pay, and pay for statutory holidays, subject to the approval of the war labour board.

A standing committee of two representatives of the publisher and two representatives of the union shall be appointed. To this committee shall be referred all disputes which may arise as to the construction to be placed upon any clause or clauses of this agreement, or alleged violation thereof which cannot be settled otherwise. Such committee shall meet within five days when any question of difference shall have been referred to it for decision by either party to this agreement. Should the standing committee be unable to agree unanimously within ten days, then it shall refer the disputed clause or clauses to a board of arbitration. The representatives of each party to this agreement shall select two arbiters, the four to agree upon a fifth who shall be a disinterested party, a resident of Ottawa. If the two representatives of each of the two parties to this agreement fail to agree upon the fifth member to complete the board of arbitration, the Ontario Minister of Labour shall be asked to name a fifth member who shall act as chairman. The majority decision of this board shall be final and binding upon both parties and the cost of such arbitration to be borne equally by the union and the publisher. Provided that the local and international laws of the union, which are a part of this agreement, shall not be subject to arbitration, except insofar as such arbitration and the results thereof are compulsory under Canadian laws, or except where said laws specifically permit their submission to arbitration.
Either party to this agreement may notify the other party thirty (30) days prior to the termination date that it desires to negotiate a revision of the terms of this agreement. If such notice is given, it shall signify that the terms of such revision shall become effective immediately upon the termination date herein set forth and, if not agreed upon by that time, shall be retroactive to the said termination date. Failure of either party to notify the other party, as above stated, shall signify that the terms of the present agreement are to remain in full force and effect until thirty (30) days after the date of termination. If negotiations fail to result in a mutual satisfactory settlement, the matter shall be referred to arbitration as specified in the foregoing paragraph. (It is agreed that section 5, article 2, I.T.U. general laws shall not apply to a joint standing committee dispute except as the union laws may be involved, but said section shall apply to arbitration of a succeeding agreement.)

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL, COMMITTEE ON REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
I have been looking at some of the reports of special committees set up by the house to deal with special problems during the session. One which I desire to bring to the attention of the leader of the house rather than yourself, Your Honour, although you are the chairman of it, is the special committee dealing with the revision of standing orders of the House of Commons. While it is late in the session, yet I think attention should be directed to the fact that the first report of the committee was made on April 10 of this year. So far as I know, no proceedings have been taken to ask for concurrence in the report, which dealt with two major matters; first, a revision of the rules with respect to protracted debates, which I fancy would at once engage the
[Mr. Mitchell.)
enthusiastic attention of the country and of parliament, and second, the proposed reference of estimates to standing, select or special committees. I should like to ask the leader of the government, first, if there is any intention to have concurrence moved in the first report; second, what has happened to the committee since its first	report,-because I	have	noiheard of it since; and third, if somehow or other before the next session of parliament agreement may be made in the house to	the end that what has	happenedin	so many	previous sessions	will	notbe	repeated.	I refer particularly to	the
fact that although we have a large volume of work, there is a lack of organization in the House of 'Commons. I do not say that in any critical way, but rather with the idea of trying to see if we cannot organize our business in such a manner as to have it in keeping with conditions in the twentieth century rather than conditions of the nineteenth century.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): The hon. member knows how jealous each hon. member is, and properly so, of the traditional privileges he enjoys as a member of parliament. Among those who sit on this side of the house, and I am sure it must be the same with respect to hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side, many discussions have taken place as to what would be a proper method of arranging to expedite, in perhaps what would appear to make a more businesslike way, the affairs of the house without unduly impinging on the traditional rights of individual members. It is a serious problem, because hon. members are not only concerned with their present rights and privileges but feel a responsibility towards future parliaments. In conversation I found a great reluctance to take the responsibility of cutting down any of the traditional privileges of individual members. That is a responsibility which each one of us feels. It is for that reason that there has been no proposal of concurrence in the first report of the committee. It has appeared to me that it would be extremely difficult to get agreement about which everyone would feel comfortable on any general modification of the rules of the house.
I have discussed with others the possibility of having partial measures provided for by a resolution which would be effective only for the duration of a session. I think certain procedures could be arranged by way of resolution adopted at the beginning of a session which would be binding only for the duration

Labour Conditions
of the session and would not make members feel that they were definitely abandoning any of their traditional rights and privileges. The experience which would be gained under that kind of resolution might point the way to something more permanent which could be done later.
One suggestion which has been made is that at the opening of parliament, instead of having a resolution to give precedence to the debate on the address over all other matters until the address is ultimately adopted, it might be decided that following the speeches of the leaders on the address the debate would have precedence only from eight o'clock in the evening, so that from three o'clock until six ordinary business could be proceeded with, the committees could be set up, bills could be introduced and considered and much of the ordinary work done during the afternoon sitting without depriving any hon. member of the opportunity of speaking on the address, but merely asking him to do so between eight o'clock and eleven o'clock until the address should be disposed of. That is one suggestion that has been made, which could be brought about by a resolution effective for only one session. The experiment might indicate whether or not something of the kind would enable a great deal of the work to get under way before the expiry of the three and sometimes four weeks it takes to dispose of the debate on the address. I would hope that at the opening of the next session an attempt might be made by way of resolutions, of which this could be just an illustration or example, to make provision for that session, without any hon. member feeling that he was giving up, not only for himself only but for future parliamentarians, any of the traditional rights we have enjoyed up to the present time.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs based upon a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in several newspapers this morning predicting what might almost be described as a wholesale shuffle in the External Affairs department, concerning some five or six of the most prominent men in that department. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice, who is handling this department, if he has any comment to make in this connection, because the dispatch deals with some of the vacant diplomatic posts both in Canada and abroad. May I point out to the minister that five of the major posts in our diplomatic service have been vacant for periods up to six months, and I believe we should have some comment from the government as to what is to be done to fill them.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): I thank the hon. member for raising this question; I had intended to refer to the dispatch in any event. My attention had been called to this Canadian Press dispatch in the morning papers of to-day concerning possible changes in the headship of Canadian missions abroad. This story is a mixture of speculation and inaccuracies. No decisions have been taken by the government on the filling of posts abroad which are now vacant. The final paragraph of the story reads as follows:
Vacancies include the high commissioner offices in Canberra. Wellington. St. John's, Dublin and New Delhi and missions in several European countries.
I may comment that there are no vacancies m the high commissioner posts in Wellington and St. John's, which are filled by Mr. A. V. Rive and Mr. J. S. Macdonald respectively. There is no high commissioner's office in New Delhi. There are no vacancies in any of the Canadian diplomatic missions on the continent of Europe. I might also take this occasion to deny a report which appeared a few days ago to the effect that the Canadian ambassador
[Mr. Lmv.l
to Belgium was about to be appointed to the post of ambassador in Paris. There is no foundation for that report.
With respect to the suggestions that there have been some delays in making appointments, I may say to the hon. member and to the house that this is a matter of definite policy. It is the purpose of the Department of External Affairs to have as many as possible of these posts filled by career men. Of course our expansion has been such that it has not been possible in every instance to promote career men to these posts; but a career man who has a secondary post in a mission is given valuable experience by being called upon to act as charge d'affaires for a period, and he is deliberately allowed to continue to carry on as such in order to give him an opportunity of demonstrating his fitness for promotion to higher office. As the hon. member knows, our requirements in connection with representation abroad have grown very rapidly, and it has not been always possible to provide enough career men, but the policy being pursued by the department is to train career men as rapidly as that can be done. I am happy to be able to say that a large number of brilliant young men from the armed forces have, since the beginning of demobilization, been absorbed into the Department of External Affairs, and are proving to be very good material for the responsibilities which have to be discharged in representing Canada abroad.

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very reasonable approach to the problem of peacetime industrial relations, if one recalls the experience which we have had during the war yeaTS, and on the other hand the exigencies of the days that lie ahead.
Among others we had, during the war, order in council P.C. 1003, better known as the national labour code, which came into effect March 20, 1944. It had arisen from a consultation with the provinces, and with the national presidents of the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the national syndicates and the railway brotherhoods. Its purpose and effect *was to clarify the rights of the workers and of the employers, to make collective bargaining obligatory, to impose penalties against interference with employees' union activities, and to eliminate the necessity of striking for union recognition. It may be that this code did not bring all the good results which were expected at first, but it remains that it has contributed to a great extent to improvement of the relations between management and labour, to better substantially the lot of the workers, and to increase our war production to the high level which it has known.
The committee must be supported in its recommendation that a dominion-provincial labour conference be called at the earliest possible moment. It is suggested, and properly so, that the federal government take the initiative of calling this conference together. Who else could do so with as much authority? I do not see any serious reason why any province should not accept such an invitation spontaneously, and should not come here with an open mind to discuss the problem of industrial relations in each province and put together the experiences whioh they have had in their respective sections of the country within the past few years.

Industrial Relations
Why put the emphasis on the diversity of the conditions which prevails across the country? I agree that they must be taken into serious account in the study of any problem of national significance. Why not rather put together all that the provinces have in common, either as to doctrine or as to experience, and set up a common basis for the enactment of labour legislation which will take care of the minimum requirements for the promotion of industrial peace in this country?
Similar conferences should thereafter be held regularly with a view to keeping these preliminary agreements on the level of actual exigencies.
When I recall the founding of the international labour organization after the first great war and the priceless services it has rendered since in the promotion of social justice in all the countries of the world, I do not see why a closer association of our provincial governments could not achieve the same end within this country. The international labour organization held until 1939 twenty-five sessions and adopted sixty-seven conventions and sixty-six recommendations. The conventions have secured nearly nine hundred formal ratifications by governments, and dealt with hours of work; holidays with pay; regulation of conditions of work of women; protection of child workers; prevention of and compensation for industrial accidents; insurance against unemployment, sickness, old age and death; apprenticeship and training for employment; colonial labour problems; living and working conditions of seamen at sea and ashore. What the international labour office has done and still can do by mutual agreement between the nations of the world for the promotion of social justice and the establishment of a better understanding, it seems obvious to me, Mr. Speaker, that our country can do, within its boundaries, by closer consultation with the provinces.
The report before the house contains recommendations which, if they are translated into legislation, will constitute an important milestone in the improvement of our labour legislation. Our country has already done much in this field, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who has devoted his whole career to that great cause. We can do more, and I hope that we shall succeed, with the cooperation of all parties concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my privilege to be a member of the industrial relations committee, and I cherish that privilege, because I have come out much wiser and greatly benefited as a result of what I learned there. I
did not go there as a labour expert; I regarded myself as one of the representatives of the general public. I may say that it was very encouraging and it increased my faith in human nature when we came to our conclusions and found men of all parties in this house getting together and working out the final basis for our report without any partisan bias whatever. I say that without equivocation.
Various comments have been made on our findings and conclusions; some of them are flattering, some not. As a matter of fact the greatest value, I believe, which came out of this committee was the general publicity which was given throughout the length and breadth of the land to labour-management affairs.
I have no particular brief for either labour or management. I think that there are good union leaders; as a matter of fact, the majority are; but on the other hand, in all fairness- and we must be fair in these matters-we must admit that there are also good employers. Throughout the industrial history of Canada and the United States, employers have done much, in many cases, to help the conditions of the employees. So that we must not put all the blame on one side. In some of the present disputes, I believe, blame is unquestionably to be put on both sides. This was proven by evidence which we heard in the committee.
We are going through what I would call the struggle for Canada's destiny. It started in 1939, and it is not over yet. I divide it into phases. There was the war; there is the transitional period; and there is the time to come. I will liken it to an attack. We have reached our first objective; we have won the war. There is no question that it is harder to win a permanent and lasting peace than it is to win a war. The fact is that such a thing as a permanent and lasting peace has never yet been won. Our second objective is winning the peace, which will mean prosperity, freedom and happiness throughout Canada. At the moment we have reached an intermediate objective, the transitional period through which we are now passing; and in order to win a final peace-I mean an industrial peace as well as a cessation of gunfire- we must be strong to go ahead.
At the present time we are beset with enemies, the enemy of inflation, the enemy of distrust, the enemy of impatience. What have we done? We cannot allow inflation to develop, and so for this intermediate objective we have formed what we call the Gordon line. The Gordon line may bend here and there; a salient may be driven into it here and there, but we cannot allow that Gordon line to break. If we do, the enemy inflation will break through the gap and
Industrial Relations

swallow up the farmer, the fisherman, the pensioner and all people living on small earned incomes. We cannot allow that to happen, and so we in this House of Commons have to be the cohorts of Mr. Gordon to help him hold the line. As I say, the line may have to bend a little here and there. All right; how are we going to advance from there?
In modern warfare you put down a heavy artillery fire preparatory to your ground forces moving ahead to the next objective. What is our plan to be? Press relations, informing the public as to what is going on, are very important. Our artillery in holding the Gordon line consists of the press. The large city newspapers lay down the heavy artillery, and the small town dailies and the country newspapers, weeklies and magazines are the medium and field artillery. What do you do in an attack? You direct all your artillery to the main target area. That is just what we must do. We must direct our artillery fire in a definite direction; the fire must be properly directed and be accurate. Therefore I say to the press: direct your fire properly to the right target and be sure you direct it accurately.
So far as the committee is concerned the press, generally speaking, particularly those members of it who sat in from day to day at our meetings, was accurate and fair, but there have been many editorials that have been unfair and I have seen unfair criticisms. We must remember that the rounds that fall short are the dangerous ones. One or two rounds did fall short and pretty nearly hit the Minister of (Labour (Mr. Mitchell) but did him no harm because he looks hale and hearty still. But it was most unfair of the press to let those rounds fall short, and I hope that they will be more accurate in their fire in future. The Minister of Labour has done and is doing a good job, and we want him to stay on and to receive all the encouragement he can get. I feel reasonably optimistic about the future, because Canada is a great country. Canadians are wonderful people individually, and all we have to do is to learn to be that way collectively. The press, properly directed, can help to bring that about. I have great faith in the future of Canada because of the press, but only by the press directing their fire accurately can we come to a happy understanding and have peace and prosperity throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
I am not going to compliment the members of the committee individually. I think they all worked hard and that they were very sincere in what they did. I could pick out
(Mr. Baker.]
certain stars of the team, but I shall not do that because the sounds they want to hear are not sweet words about themselves but the music of the humming wheels of industry turning again and friendly and civil talk between the leaders in management and labour. I maintain that the press can also help there.
I shall not take up any more time, because a good deal of the ground has already been covered and one or two able speakers are to follow me. But I did want to make that point about the press. The members of the press who were in the committee room with us working long and tedious hours were gallant gunners, and so in conclusion, with respect to labour-management relations and in their relations to the dominion government I would say: Praise the press and pass the information.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to start in by paying any compliments to the chairman or the members of the committee. My impression of the committee was that it did the best it could with the latitude it was allowed and the equipment it had to work with. I am going to try to focus the attention of the house this morning on the fact that all the hard work of that committee means nothing if the present attitude on the part of employers and the controller is to continue.
On July 16 industrial relations in this country had come to such a pass that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the eve of leaving for the peace conference in Paris accepted a suggestion from the opposition that the subject of labour relations and industrial .unrest should be placed in the hands of the industrial relations committee to see if that committee could not arrive at some formula whereby industrial disputes in this country might be resolved. When the Prime Minister accepted that invitation from this side of the house my reaction was that the machinery provided in this country by the Department of Labour was in a bad way and was being superseded because it was inadequate to handle the disputes that existed at that time. In passing that task over to the committee the Prime Minister in my opinion passed it over to all parties in this house to accept the joint responsibility of trying to resolve those difficulties and recommend some measure or formula that might prevent such disputes from taking place in the future. The committee did not do that and my opinion is that its work is not completed. It

Industrial Relations
merely skimmed the surface. It made some recommendations to this house which would be helpful if they are implemented.
It was on July 16 that this task was entrusted to the committee with the sanction of the Prime Minister. One month later, after this committee had taken all the evidence and probed behind the scenes for the reasons for the present industrial disputes, industrial unrest and the strike situation in Canada is worse to-day than it was then. To say that the committee performed any miracles when it did not change the situation in industry is not correct. In addition to the strikes that existed at the time, and they still exist, a new strike threat looms on the horizon, a strike by the packing house workers, who if their difficulties are not resolved by a certain date are going to strike on a national scale. So the committee did not accomplish very much.
I am not going to read the record but the fact is that every strike that existed on July 16 when the committee was set up is still in existence, including the steelworkers' strike.
The first night that the committee met for organization purposes a motion was made that we would set as our first objective the settling of the steel dispute. That objective was not accomplished. The first day on which the committee actually sat in formal session I moved that the controller appointed by the [DOT] government under order in council P.C. 2901 be instructed to exercise his duties under that order in council by beginning negotiations with the union, apart from the employers, and endeavouring to resolve their difficulties here in Ottawa while the committee was taking evidence.
That motion was not accepted, but lay on the table three days, and the committee finally decided that the employers should get together despite the fact that they had no longer any authority in the management of the steel industry, since the government had superseded their executive authority by the appointment of a controller; and1 despite that legal technicality the employers and employees had been together month after month and had not successfully resolved the difficulty. They precipitated the strike, and in my opinion it was bad technique and unsound judgment to expect them, because they were in the atmosphere of Ottawa, to get together and resolve the difficulty. In my opinion valuable time was wasted and the legality or validity of that order in council, or any order in council in the future, can be challenged if the attitude taken by the government with regard to its enforcement in that particular instance was valid.
I say we wasted a lot of time and the committee did not attain the first objective they
set themselves in the settlement of the steel dispute. That is very important, because the steel industry in Canada has now a basic strike on hand. Steel ramifies all through our economy, and if a determined and reasonable attempt had been made to resolve the steel difficulty, in my opinion the formula arrived at there would automatically be applied to the other difficulties that exist in industry, and we would have been straightening out the whole picture at one time. But we are back in the house with no recommendation on the basic issue in dispute.
The steelworkers before the committee made a sound and reasonable case. They showed that they were not adamant in their attitude. They modified their position on two occasions. I felt that when the controller finally came into the picture the committee should have recommended to him the last proposal made by the steelworkers' union to the committee and to the employers and to Mr. Brockington, who was acting then as mediator in the dispute. That should have gone forward to the controller as a reasonable basis for negotiations, but that was not done, so that the controller was in the same position that Mr. Brockington was in. He goes back in there with the ten cent formula over his head and with very little latitude and very little possibility of settling the difficulty unless someone is prepared to do some plain talking on the part of the government.

The general impression is that the industrial workers are demanding wage increases. That is not the case. The industrial workers to-day, because of the failure to hold the price line, are asking for increases in their basic rates in order that they may maintain the income they had during the war. That is all they are doing. I am going to put the last proposal of the steelworkers' union on the record. It is very simple. The first is the removal of the five-cent Sydney differential. That is a case that has been before the national war labour board and the regional boards for the last three years. It is still before the national board. It was turned down three times. In my opinion it should not be included in this dispute. I suggest that the Minister of Labour, who has some authority over the national war labour board, in order to get that particular problem out of the way, and separated from the basic problem in the Sydney plant, might suggest that they make a decision in that case and remove one of the sore spots as far as the Sydney plant is concerned.
Industrial Relations

The second of their proposals was a general wage increase of ten cents an hour retroactive to April 1, 19415, in the primary steel plants and the fabricating plants of all three operating companies. That is a very reasonable proposal. The national director of the steelworkers' union, in presenting his case to the committee, recognized the fact that while the plants and production are tied up, the danger of inflation is increased fifty per cent. He was not asking for his total demands at that time. He was prepared to take it in stages and to accept and recommend at once the ten cents to his membership, so that the plants might get back into production and lessen the dangers of inflation.
The next proposal with regard to wages was adjustments totalling 5-J cents an hour to compensate for increases in the cost of living from April 1 to July 1, such adjustments to be payable this calendar year. I consider that one of the most important recommendations made by the steelworkers' union. I am of that opinion for this reason, that it is a weapon in the hands of the wartime prices and trade board if they want to maintain prices.

You will increase the cost of living and you are going to adjust the wages of your workers in proportion to the increased cost of living." It is the only weapon that has been suggested to date which would assist in maintaining prices in this country, but the committee did not see it that way.
Number four on the agenda was that all the other issues in dispute to be completed by October, 1946, should go to arbitration. The date to which the removal of the Sydney differential should be made retroactive was backed up on, and they proposed that it be put where it was suggested it should be in the first place; and second, the dates upon which the adjustments totalling 5| cents should be made payable were to remain in abeyance and be made the subject of arbitration. With respect to the further increases on the basis of the cost of living, one cent per point, they were also prepared to send that to arbitration. Hours of work, overtime pay for statutory holidays, vacations with pay, a union security formula applicable to all plants-these were all to go to arbitration, and in effect the

immediate proposal made, the one that would start the plants in operation if accepted, was the removal of the Sydney differential, and the general increase of ten cents an hour retroactive to April 1, 1946 in the primary steel plants and the fabricating plants of the three operating companies.
That would settle the steel strike, and the other matters would go to arbitration. I believe Mr. Millard, the national director of the steelworkers' union, was much fairer than many others I know of in a similar position in trying to get that industry into operation. Nevertheless, so far as the committee was concerned I do not think he succeeded. If hon. members will read the evidence presented and the document to which I have referred I do not think that they will say that the case presented by the steelworkers' union with respect to the adjustment of wages is unreasonable. It is not an increase in wages; it is an endeavour to maintain the take-home pay of those in these industries who have lost that percentage of their take-home pay because of the increase in prices.
When I hear hon. members say that the price ceilings must be maintained, I agree. I said that from the start; we have all said it. But the fact of the matter is that they have not been maintained. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) recognizes why the cost of living bonus was established in the first place. It was established to hold the price line; it was one of the most important parts of the whole mechanism. The cost of living bonus was worked into the basic rates. It was taken off, and in my opinion that was the initial mistake. Immediately that took place there was pressure largely from the manufacturers in Canada for increases in the prices of basic commodities, and that started the drive on the price ceiling. The wartime prices and1 trade board, reacting to that pressure, in my opinion, removed the ceilings literally from hundreds of commodities. Before the last election the start was made when the twenty-five per cent luxury tax was taken off vacuum cleaners, washing machines and all of these things which are essentials to the average householder.

He may say that; theoretically it is true, but practically it is not, because if Donald Gordon suggests a ceiling on wages beyond which you cannot go without endangering the economy of the country, then Donald Gordon is supreme in the matter of fixing wages, because everyone else has to work under that ceiling. While theoretically he says that another board sets the wages, nevertheless he is placing a ceiling under which this board must work; therefore Gordon is supreme. He may say that he does not sit in and make decisions, but he tells you the point beyond which you are not allowed to go. I want to emphasize that. Wages to-day are not chasing prices and endangering the economy of the country by inflation. The reverse is true. Prices have gone up and wages are trying to chase them in order to maintain the standards established during the war. The responsibility is not on the industrial workers; it is on those who did not maintain the price ceiling. I emphasize that, because according to the evidence given before the committee it is absolutely correct.
On this matter of inflation I would like to say this, while we are at it. Sometimes it amazes me how glibly some people can talk about it when it affects someone else. I wonder how many hon. members ever stop to think of this. The wage increases in steel would create perhaps about $15,000,000 of additional purchasing power in this country, or something like that. Did we cry inflation when the government proposed, and rightly so, to spend $250,000,000 a year for family allowances? They placed $250,000,000 a year of extra purchasing power in the hands of a class of our society who do not produce anything, a class who are going to school. The proposition was absolutely right, but Donald Gordon did not cry inflation at that time; it was quite all right. On the other hand when we lent hundreds of millions of dollars to Britain and other countries, of which a large proportion was to be spent in Canada-and rightly so; I supported those loans-there was no cry of inflation, though these millions of dollars of extra purchasing power were to be spent in this country to take goods out of this 
country. Now the government propose to increase the salaries of judges to $15,000 or $20,000 a year, which is extra purchasing power to a class of our society who do not produce consumer goods, but that is quite all right; there is no cry of inflation.

If the statement made in this telegram is true; if the controller took that line of action m Hamilton, that controller should be replaced, because this committee definitely condemned, in no uncertain terms, the use of physical force by either employer or employee in any dispute. If this man issued these orders, that trucks were to be driven
through those picket lines, endangering the lives of those men at this particular stage in this dispute, he should be replaced. If he is not replaced you will find no solution to the difficulty in Hamilton or in basic steel. If he made the statement that he was going to take an inventory of everyone in these plants, then the man is not competent to act in the dispute he has authority to handle, and should be replaced. I do not know whether or not these things are true. The vice-president of the Hamilton works may not be telling the truth; it. may be just a technique to try and smash the picket line, but the minister should check, and if the controller has taken that line of action he should be removed.
Let us look at the other side of the picture, with regard to violations of law and order. When a strike takes place the press, the heavy artillery which was mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Baker)-he depends upon the press to pull us out of our difficulties-are always on the other side. With all due respect to those who work for the press, I have found that in their opinion the worker is always wrong, that he is always in an illegal position. If you want the workers of this country to obey the law, then employers also must be made to obey the law and set the example. See what you have there in Hamilton in the way of law violations by the employers. In the first place they were permitted-and Donald Gordon should be checked on this- to inveigle men and women into that plant by paying them three times the wages they received previously, under normal operations. In that plant they are paid for twenty-four hours a day. That is an incentive to bring them in. It is a violation of the labour laws of this country, if that company did not get permission from the war labour board. When the minister replies I should like him to say whether the Steel Company of Canada did get permission to increase by three times the wages of those who are now in the plant in Hamilton, whether that was done with the permission of the war labour board.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: The hon. member is talking about clause 6?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Yes. The intention behind clause 6, according to my interpretation and my understanding of it in committee, and also as I remember it-the Minister of Reconstruction placed himself on record last night as to his understanding of it-was that we were trying to adopt a provision under which the working men in this country when they are asked to place their wives and families up against a picket line-because they are the ones who will do the suffering-should have a
right to vote on it. If an industry is to go on a strike in this country, the merits or demerits of the dispute or strike action should be balloted on by those affected in the industry -the man who, in the final analysis, pays the bill. Secondly, as to the latter part of it, my conception of it was this, that if a vote is taken, as it has been taken in this steel dispute, that legalizes that strike as far as the vote is concerned. If an industry is tied up without a vote having been taken, it is not only the prerogative of the Minister of Labour but it is his duty as a responsible member of the government to see that a vote is taken to determine the wishes of the people affected in that particular dispute. Many constructions were put upon this in the house, and every hon. member is entitled to exercise his judgment as to what this section means. I know what I meant when I supported it. I had the word of the Minister of Labour that he would make a statement in the house and put that interpretation on the record.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Just a question for the purpose of clarification. I believe I am thinking along the same line as my hon. friend. Take such a case as I pointed out in the committee; that I receive a report from either side and after investigation I am of the opinion that the vote was not taken properly -my hon. friend knows what I am driving at-[DOT] we would not put that outside the discretion of the minister?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Not at all. If I were minister of labour and I was told that an industry with 14,000 workers had taken a vote in a telephone booth by a show of hands, I would certainly see that a proper vote was taken- definitely. But the particular angle of the thing which I am concerned about is this, that the right to say whether you are going to strike should rest with the rank and file affected. That is where it should rest. That is democracy'. On the other hand, if men are pulled out on wild-cat strikes the minister of labour in this country cannot be a rubber stamp. Suppose I wxere the responsible minister; I could not see myself accepting a position whereby someone pulls the pin from under an industry and walks in and says to me, "We are on strike, whether you like it or not, and we are running the show without any consultation with the rank and file of the people of this country." The basis of the movement which I belong to is control on the part of the people. That is why we hold conventions and write policies. The leadership of this C.C.F. movement carries out the instructions given by the rank and file.

Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I would like to say that the mechanism of the particular matter we are talking about is not for the benefit of us in Nova Scotia. We take that vote; there is no trade union leader in the province who, on any of the basic issues which affect the membership of the union, would dare take any step without a referendum vote-a levy on membership, a strike, agreements when they are finalized. That is democracy, and that is what we fight to retain. I was called from Sydney a few nights ago when this was phoned to them. Some one interpreted this proposal as meaning that the Minister of Labour could order a vote in the Hamilton plant on the wage question. It cannot be done. After a vote is taken it legalizes the strike; if there is not a vote there should not be a strike.
The hon, member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) spoke of the Rand formula. I am all for the Rand formula. I would have written it in the report; and I may add that if I had. written that report it wTould have been different from what it is. There would have been about four clauses in it, strong and specific. But no one member wrote it; it was a compromise, based on different opinions. But when the hon. member for Spadina said the other evening that the Rand formula would apply to this situation and would cure it, I must tell him that it has nothing to do with it. The Rand formula is union security; this is a strike vote. If the Rand formula is applied to industry in this country it eliminates picketing. There is proof of that in the steel strike. In Sydney there is no picketing, because they are organized one hundred per cent and they have union security by agreement.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Is that not the best kind of security?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Definitely. And there is no picketing at Algoma. There is no union security in Stelco, but there is a civil war on. I would say that the Minister of Labour should have a national code enacted as soon as possible and write into it the Rand formula or something like it. On the other hand, the hon. member for Spadina based his construction of this particular section on the use of the' word "affected". I do not know what he has in mind. I had no intention of including the superintendents, clerical staff, stenographers and so on. They are not affected. In any strike I have ever been in, the office staffs and superintendents and clerical staffs and
fMr. Gillis]
confidential staffs were paid their salaries, and they are not eligible for membership in the union. But I think that every man who is eligible for membership in the organization should have the right to vote, because he is affected and should be consulted,

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Would you go this far; would you use the constitution of the organization-?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Definitely. These things are written into the constitution and the agreements of the old established unions. But in this province you have not old established unions except in the crafts, and in your mass industries, particularly, until such time as they have grown to maturity and write these laws for themselves in their own agreements and constitutions, legislative action is necessary now, in order to guide them and see that the rank and file-and, indeed, the leadership-are protected. Because pressure groups in an organization can throw a strike against the wishes of the executive board; they wake up in the morning and find their industry is tied up and they have had nothing to say about it; then they are "behind the eight ball" in disentangling it.
This is not legislation; this is merely a suggestion by way of a report from this committee. I assume that officers of the crown will sit in and draft legislation on the basis of these recommendations. All legislation which goes through this house is prepared in that manner; regulations are written, interpretation clauses provided, and so on. All this is merely a suggestion. We did not try to write legislation. I had no conception or thought of doing so. Under present circumstances in this country I am merely supporting number 6 on the assumption that the construction placed on it by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and the Minister of Labour in the committee, and the ideas I have about it, are correct. It is to provide for a strike vote; before an industry goes on strike, balloting the men affected, and then there is the "after" business, after a strike takes place, after an industry has pulled a strike without consultation by ballot of the men affected the minister has a duty to perform to take a ballot there and see that it is taken properly; and that is the end of it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: If the minister has any doubt as to how the ballot was taken?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Yes. If you are notified by the membership that no proper ballot was taken, certainly you have a duty to perform. Then, I think, either side should be in a position to demand it. There may be cases in which you will get as many requests from

Industrial Relations
the employees of an industry as you will from the industrialists, that they are on strike without a ballot. I could tell you of many of these things which I have been through, but I do not want to waste time. That is why we have written these provisions into our constitutions and our agreements. When the minister speaks I want him to clarify that particular point. I am supporting the proposal on that basis: it is a strike vote and a strike vote only. I use the word "affected" because I believe it is important. It would place trade union leadership in this position, that before a strike took place in any industry which they were organizing they would be absolutely sure that they had a reasonable number of people in the organization to make that strike successful. Striking a split plant Is bad tactics, and I believe that the people should be guided with legislation of this kind to make sure that a proper organizational job is done before a strike. I think some of us who have had experience here should have the courage to put that into legislative form as a guide to those who, if we do so, will not have to learn the hard way, the way that some of us had to learn it.
In conclusion, and I apologize for taking so much time, there are three things that must be done. First, if this man Kilbourn has made the statements attributable to him here with regard to Hamilton and the way he intends to take an inventory of every person in the plant, he should be removed. Otherwise he has scrapped our committee's work. Second, I think that someone who is fair and who has not got something like that on him should be appointed and that the steelworkers' last proposal should be used as a basis of negotiations for settlement. Their three proposals if accepted would settle the strike and the rest could be left to arbitration. But the important thing is to get the industry back into production as quickly as possible. Many of the committee's recommendations could be worked out later, but it is essential that the industry be got back into production as soon as possible. I think the Minister of Labour should give serious consideration to the recommendation of the union that industrial councils be set up to deal directly with management, employees and the government. They should replace the present war labour boards, which were set up as a war measure and were designed for a different period. They are not measuring up to the requirements of this period. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to that.
I wanted to place my opinions on the record. I respect the opinions of others who may have disagreed with me on clause 6; for I
know that they all want to do the best they can for those affected. I hope that the interpretations as I understand them and as the Minister of Labour understands them and as the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply understands them will be written into legislation to be presented to the house for the guidance of union people and industrialists in this country.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.
Mr. C. E. JOHNSTON (Bow River)': Mr. Speaker, the question that we were discussing before the house rose is one in which every hon. member is deeply interested, and I do not think it can be said that any one member is more concerned about it than another. It is a question that affects the whole economy of Canada, and certainly I believe that everyone else is just as anxious as I am to have the strike settled. As I was a member of the committee and also of the steering committee, I believe that the members of both sides, the main committee and the subcommittee as well, were sincere in the work they performed. It was a difficult task, and it was made difficult because of the fact that the strike was already in progress. It was made difficult too because of the limitations of the order of reference to the committee. I do not believe, and I am sure many other members of the committee feel as I do, that the order was wide enough to cover the field as efficiently and as thoroughly as it should have been. Moreover the time factor was an important part in our proceedings, because the house was due to close, or at least we hoped it would close, within a very short time, and we were compelled under the order of reference to report back to the house. That was an important factor in accounting for the short report which the committee made to the house.
Some people may think, looking over the committee's report, that there is not much substance in it. On the contrary I believe that if the recommendations are followed by the government a great deal of good can come from the report, and I wish to pay tribute to the members of the main committee and the steering committee-I was one of them-for their sincerity in desiring to bring the committee's deliberations to a satisfactory conclusion.
I have looked at the papers this morning and it seems to be the opinion of some at least that the members who speak from this
Industrial Relations

I say that is not according to the facts. We should put the record straight in one instance. I do not wish to tire the house at this late hour by reading long extracts from the evidence. But this is an important matter. Had it been cleared up in the first place I do not think the strike would ever have taken place. Let me read from the evidence exactly what Mr. Gordon had to say in regard to the increase in wages which was supposed to have been allowed in the $5 increase in the price of steel. There is no mistaking this evidence; Mr. Gordon was most clear and explicit. I asked him a question, and I am going to read that question together with the answer so that the committee may be in a position to judge whether or not the statement by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is in accordance with the evidence. At page 329 of the proceedings of that committee I asked:
The point I wanted to make is this, Mr. Gordon, that you were in a better position to decide whether or not this company could make a ten cent offer. The company was in a more favourable position than you were to know they could make the ten cent offer, and what was the position of the union in demanding the increase. Now, it wras quite evident

Notice this.
-that there was a certain amount in that $5 which had been allocated for wages.
The answer Mr. Gordon gave was this:
No. not necessarily: that is the point I have been labouring to put forward. That was dependent entirely on the decision of the management of the steel company as to what profit level they were willing to operate on; and they could quite easily and quite reasonably have taken the attitude that they could not afford to pay anything for wages because they were not earning a profit amount anywhere near the amount which they ought to be earning by pre-war standards in relation to the volume of production that they are now undertaking. I have already told you that the steel company had reached a production of two and a half times their pre-war volume.
A little further down, in explaining the same question, Mr. Gordon went on to say that if the company had taken the view they could not give anything

That would have been a reasonable argument. But if they had taken that stand I do not think they could have paid anything.
Then to make doubly sure, at that point the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) interjected:
-you allowed yourself to he in a position where there might have been nothing, and you say it is reasonable for them to take that position.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the remarks of the minister are not in accordance with the evidence given by Mr. Gordon.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: What minister are you referring to?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: The Minister of Reconstruction.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: For once I am out of it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Yes. If the wartime prices and trade board had done as I believe they should; if they had thoroughly investigated the financial position of the company before making any suggestion of an increase in the price of steel; if they had waited until they knew exactly what increases were to be made in wages, they would have avoided a great deal of difficulty. But the wartime prices and trade board never knew for sure whether there was anything at all, whether there was one cent or whether there was twenty-five cents for wages in the $5 rise in steel. Had the wartime prices and trade board been in a position to say to the unions, "We are allowing a S5 increase, in which there is a ten cent increase in wages," and had this offer of the ten cent wage increase been made at the time the $5 increase in price was permitted, I believe our difficulties would have been avoided. But there was absolutely no relation between the price increases granted the steel company and the wages offered the steel workers. In my view there should be a more definite and thorough investigation into that problem, and certainly into the relationship between the wartime prices and trade board and the national war labour board.
In my opinion the wartime prices and trade board started from the wrong point in this matter. When they made the offer of $5 they were developing their negotiations with Stelco, which is financially better off than any of the other companies. It seems to me they should have begun their negotiations with the company in the poorest financial position, to ascertain whether or not they needed an increase in price and what increase would be required in order to give the workers in that plant a decent standard of living. I believe they would have saved themselves a great deal of difficulty if they had begun in that way.
If I might refer back to the quotation I read from the evidence of Mr. Gordon, that was given when Mr. Gordon was before the committee in person. Later he submitted a statement which was merely placed on the record, from which I should like to read one or two lines in order to show a contradiction in his statements. At page 4 of the statement which was placed on record he said:
As I said before, that was a departure from our usual practice. In considering every other application for a price increase, we have not taken into account the possibility of future wage increases. This steel case was an exception and

Industrial Relations
the decision was made, as I have stated in previous evidence, in the expectation that settlement of the price application would enable pending wage negotiations to be completed quickly. Furthermore, it certainly increased labour's chances of getting a reasonable and prompt increase in wages.
I say that is in absolute contradiction with the evidence he gave in person. Further down this statement says:
We authorized this increase in good faith and for good reasons and in the belief that an increase in wage rates was a certainty. .
I am quite sure that if this question had been properly dealt with in the beginning of negotiations, a great many of our difficulties never would have arisen. Then when the committee in its wisdom-properly or otherwise-decided to appoint Mr. L. W. Brock-ington as negotiator between, the companies and the union, a motion was made that the committee rise while those negotiations were taking place. That motion was supported by two or three or four of us on the committee, but was not carried. I thought it a shame that the committee should continue to take evidence during the very time the negotiating parties were endeavouring to reach a settlement. Our stand was vindicated later. The Minister of Labour, the Minister of Reconstruction and the Acting Minister of Finance gave it as their view, in public statements, that a ten cent increase was about as much as the ceiling would stand.

speechtext:
This is the point I am trying to bring out, that when the committee appointed Mr. Brockington to negotiate, the government, in effect-and the minister may take exception to this-stated government policy when it agreed with Mr. Gordon that
ten cents was about the highest that the price structure would stand. I am trying to put it fairly so that the minister will not take objec-ion to it. And that is the very thing that tied the hands of Mr. Brockington. He went into those negotiations bound by a ten-cent ceiling. The result was that when Mr. Brockington brought in his report it was evident throughout that he made a stand at ten cents. Of course the members of the union would not accept that, because they had already made public statements that they would not accept anything less than fifteen cents. The companies on the other hand had said they would not accept anything higher than ten cents. That was bound to destroy the negotiations between the company and the unions under Mr. Brockington's leadership. That procedure, which was directed by the committee itself, was doomed to failure before it ever got a chance.
Now, regardless of the fact that some may say the union is all to blame in this, I do not think that the union is all to blame. They did things which I think most hon. members think would have been better left undone. They have broken the law, as has been pointed out by other hon. members-and I am not going to repeat it. But so has the company broken the law. That will not settle our difficulties. The way to settle them is to get the two together and have a settlement made so that production will again begin to roll off the lines.
It was pointed out in committee that the companies themselves have gone into a production sit-down strike. That is something I think should be looked into, because the unions are not the only ones who are holding up production. I believe that from the point of view of inflation there is a greater danger right now of inflation coming about because of no production than there would have been if we had given the fifteen cents asked by labour. I repeat that there is a greater danger of inflation by no production than there would have been if we had granted the fifteen cents, and set up some other means of meeting the cost.
Of course some hon. members have strong objections to the government paying subsidies. I wish to point out that even in the United States the government saw fit-probably it was compelled to do so-to withdraw some of its subsidies and to withdraw price controls. But in its wisdom it has reverted to its first process. And it might be well for us in this country to revert to the giving of subsidies, now cancelled, in order to keep the wheels of production gcing. It has been drawn
Industrial Relations

to my attention, too, that tariffs are one of the greatest sources of subsidies enjoyed by industry. We allow them to be paid.
Only this afternoon I saw in to-day's issue of the Ottawa Citizen of August 21 a dispatch from Washington, dated August 20, stating:
The United States price decontrol board tonight ordered ceilings restored on all meat, and Paul Porter, head of the office of price administration, said they will be "at or close to June 30 levels."
The board ruled that dairy products and nearly all grains should remain free of ceilings but it restored price controls on soy beans and cottonseed products.
O.P.A. and the agriculture department will determine the ceilings on the recontrolled items and put them into effect Friday.
The board also authorized revival of June 29 subsidy payments on meats and live stock.
But when we suggest it might be better for the government to restore some of the subsidies in order to make it possible to meet the wage demands that labour is asking, some hon. members say, "Oh, you are crazy." But is it more dangerous to allow industry to cease producing than it would be for us to spend a few million dollars in subsidies to make up this deficiency, if the companies cannot do it? And, mind you. I do not agree that they all cannot do it, by an.y manner of means. I think it would be good business for the government and the country at least to study thfe possibility of giving subsidies in cases where they are needed. I am not going to discuss where the government will get the money to pay subsidies. It will be said that it will be raised by taxation and that it will increase the cost of living for everybody. That may be true, but at least it will be spreading it over the whole' of Canada. I should like an answer to that.
I am not going to deal with the report at length, but I would refer to one other recommendation which has been mentioned in this debate, namely section 6. I am not speaking as an experienced union man, because I am not a union man, and I want that clearly understood. But we had men on the com-mitte who were union men. We listened most carefully to union pleas in this connection, and we also listened to the side of industry too. Those of us who were impartial could at least form some logical conclusions respecting this section. So that there may be no misunderstanding for anyone who reads Hansard, I shall put the section on record. It states:
6.	Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may, at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under govern-
ment supervision to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
I was one who supported that; there were others who did not. Srime say that you can interpret it in one way, others that you can interpret it in another. I shall tell the house how I interpret it, and I believe if the government follows the recommendation as it is worded there will be no danger in it; in fact I believe it will be beneficial both to labour and to industry. My view is that in respect of what are generally called wild-cat strikes, where there has been no proper strike vote taken, even though a strike may be in progress-and that is where the words "before or after" come in-some authority may come in and take a vote to establish whether or not the negotiating party has the right to call a strike. That is my view of it. I do not think the wording of the recommendation would permit the Minister of Labour or anybody else to go in after an official strike vote has been taken, and then put on a series of votes to see whether or not the men should go back to work, when a company might desire to increase the wages by one cent or two cents or three cents or whatever they might think they could get across. That is not my view.
I am firmly of the opinion that in this instance the Minister of Labour will accept the recommendation as it is worded, and that he will go into a plant where he is satisfied a proper vote has not been taken by those affected. He will take that vote, in the manner in which any other democratic election is carried on-by secret ballot. In this way he will determine whether or not there should be a. strike. Once that strike vote has been taken, that is the end of it. The strike is in progress or it is not in progress, as the case may be.
I certainly would not agree with the view that the government should go in and interfere with the union once a strike has been properly called, and I do not believe the Minister of Labour would take that view. Certainly it would not be my view. But I do believe if the government sees fit to put the recommendations made into effect-and there are seven of them

they will be of considerable assistance in the state of industrial unrest which prevails in Canada.	.

The war labour board; I am

I think that the absence of it is at the root of this strike. Union members lack any knowledge of how far the government will permit increases in wages to go.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend, when he speaks of "wage policy", mean that we should set a sum?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Well, the government has said that there must be a measure of wage stabilization. I think it is only fair that if wages are to be stabilized to a certain degree, the government should tell the people of Canada to what level wages can be permitted to rise in this country. It does not mean necessarily that' every plant in Canada will pay 15i cents per hour more to its workers. The unions know that some plants cannot afford to pay that much. But I think you have to set a ceiling.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the ceiling is always the floor.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Yes; well, it is not the minimum. wage we are talking about now. We are in favour of a minimum wage as well.
The wartime prices and trade board, have placed a ceiling on consumer goods in this country, and every housewife and every citizen knows what that ceiling is. How the government say that we require a measure of wage stabilization in Canada, and they have to nut a ceiling on that wage stabilization if they want to get some stability into the situation.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said that he feels that the basic issues are unchanged. His remark when we came out of the committee was that the basic issues were unchanged and the thing was just where it was when we went into it.
I agree with him in that. I do not think that a thing has been changed; I think it has been aggravated to a certain extent. But that was not the committee's fault. I believe he will agree with me that we tried in every way we knew how to get the facts and to have the government make a statement on this subject, but every time we were stopped. We were stopped by Mr. Gordon's "ten cent" speech; we were stopped by a statement from the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), we were stopped by a statement from Mr. Murchison, of the Department of Labour, when he brought in a document purporting to prove that a ten cent rise in wages in Canada is equal to a 18J cent rise of wages in the United States. So in the end1 we all became, I think, a little bit discouraged.
What is the basic issue at the present time? Isn't it that? These men in Hamilton struck against their company for an increase in wages-something which organized labour all over the world can do if they so wish, They struck against their plant, whether rightly or wrongly I would not wish to argue now. But what did the government do? The government so manoeuvred the situation as to place themselves in the position of the company, so that the men are almost literally striking against the government when they meant to strike against their employers. The government is behind all these negotiations; the government has said that a measure of wage stabilization is necessary; and I have risen this afternoon only to say that it is my firm view that the government must make known the ceiling on wages.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Te-miscouata): Mr. Speaker, I was appointed to this committee, but I could not attend the sittings very regularly, for obvious reasons. I wish to congratulate the chairman for the able manner in which he presided over the proceedings of the committee. He has done exceptionally well. His task was difficult, because the committee was very large and the matters with which it dealt were most contentious; no one could have done better than he did. My praise goes also to my fellow members of the committee, all of whom were men of good will, who showed that they considered the situation a very serious one, and each of whom, in his own way, did his best to come to some agreement and offer worthwhile proposals to settle our difficulties.
This is the time-at the end of the session- to discuss the reports of all committees, but I regret very much that the estimates have not yet been passed, because there are many things which I would have said on the esti-
Industrial Relations

mates but which I shall have to say to-day. I have noticed that at the beginning of the session, when members are about to talk on a certain departmental matter they are often told they should wait until the estimates come and then they will be given a full opportunity to discuss the matter in which they are interested. But we have to wait until the end of the session; this is the 21st day of August and the session started in March, yet the estimates of the Department of Labour have not yet 'been before us.
I do not wish to praise only the work which has been done in the committee. I must eulogize hon. members who have already spoken for the tone of their speeches. Yesterday I listened to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and some others, and to-day I have listened to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and my two hon. friends who have just spoken. I congratulate them very heartily. It is impossible for all of us to have the same views about everything, and it is from discussion that we get light. The Minister of -Labour (Mr. Mitchell) should take advantage of all the suggestions which have -been offered to him to try to improve conditions of labour in this country.
In labour matters there are three parties; there is the employer, the employee, and the consumer; and, as a sagacious economist has just pointed out to me, until now the consumer has been quite a forgotten man. But I have been taught from my youth that one must respect the workers, and that they are entitled to all the comforts of life. Therefore since I have been elected a member of parliament I have done my best to try to improve the conditions of labour in this country. My first step in that regard dates back to the sessions of 1928, 1929 and 1930, when I pointed out to the House of Commons and to the government that salaries and wages in the province of Quebec were much lower than in the other provinces. During that period I never ceased to advocate fair wages and make representations to that effect to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the then minister of labour, who was Mr. Peter Heenan. I prepared tabulations showing that wages were lower in the province of Quebec than in any other province; and finally, with the support of the Prime Minister, the minister of labour sponsored a bill which is now chapter 20 of the statutes of 1930, an act respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works. Parliament did not exceed its jurisdiction, as determined by a judgment of the supreme court which was given a short time before. At [Mr. Pouliot.J
that time parliament believed in civil rights. Last year I made the suggestion during the Windsor strike that representatives of the union should be invited to attend, the committee on industrial relations, and I spoke to deaf ears. The government did not pay any attention to my suggestion; and it was only when a Conservative member repeated the same suggestion a year later, in connection with another strike, that the government jumped at it and at once accepted it. When it is offered by a Liberal it is no good; when it is offered by Conservatives it is good. I do not complain of that, because I offer my suggestions with a big heart. When they are accepted I am delighted. But what surprises me is that what comes from the party opposite is considered better than what comes from within.
In the second place I attended a sitting of the committee, and I had a chair not far from the witnesses. But then I was asked by one of the learned counsel to give him my chair. This is the first time that a member of parliament has had to give his chair up to a learned committee counsel. I am told that he was more important because his salary exceeded that paid to the counsel for the Rowell-Sirois commission by $50 a day. Therefore he was more important than a member of parliament and I had to make way for him. But I did not begrudge that. I had some business to attend to in the house. Not having the gift of ubiquity, the only thing I could do was to glance over the reports of the committee at night, and this I did not fail to do to keep myself informed of what was going on.
I want to put on record what has been done for labour by a member of parliament, and it was not done as a mission because no one had asked for it. It was a self-imposed task, undertaken to improve the conditions of labour in this country. In the first place there was the act referred to, and in the second place there was a report on unemployment. For many years I tried to bring order in the Department of Labour. During the Bennett regime the minister of labour was a big -giant, and when I suggested that classifications should be made of the unemployed he referred me to the bureau of statistics. The unemployment was prevalent in 1935, and I was referred back to statistics of the census of 1931, four years before, which was an absurdity. The Department of Labour at that time had no definite information at all about unemployment ; all the information they got was scanty.
I was told by the government of the day to go to the bureau of statistics to get the information that was not up to date but related to conditions of four years before.

Industrial Relations
But in spite of everybody and everything 1 decided to get the information I was seeking. I attended a meeting of the mayors in the Chateau Laurier and asked if the municipalities had that information. I was told by the mayor of one of the cities in western Ontario that they had, which in most cases was not true. The mayor who told me that was all wrong; it was not true. But a census of unemployment had been made by the province of Ontario at the instigation of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), who was the minister of labour and welfare in Ontario. The data I got at that time from the province of Ontario were very useful to me in the preparation of my report. What was considered an impossible thing to do by the Department of Labour at Ottawa and by the government of that day was done by the member for Temiscouata, with the aid of his secretary, in about a month and a half. It took me three weeks to collect the data from the municipalities, and another three weeks to compile it. I have the report here. When I presented it to the house I was turned down by Mr. Speaker, who said that under the rules of procedure of parliament he could not accept the report. The report had been prepared and drafted giving information as to the number of unemployed and their different trades or professions so that order might be reestablished in society and an opportunity given to the government and to municipalities and employers to put to work men who had special training or special experience. That work was done, as I said, by the member for Temiscouata, in a month and a half. It was done before the election of 1935, and I sent a copy of the report to every member of parliament, including the members supporting the government. I received a very fine letter from a Liberal candidate in northern Ontario who is now the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). His letter is dated June 19, 1935, ana reads:
Dear Mr. Pouliot:
Please accept my best thanks for copy of your memorandum dated June 8, 1935, on unemployment. I have read this with a great deal of interest, and am going through it again to make notes for use in my election campaign. It is the most complete analysis of the situation that I have. seen and will be exceedingly useful to me.
Yours sincerely,
C. D. Howe.
My report was not made -for political purposes. That was a secondary consideration. My main purpose was to bring order out of the chaotic conditions of labour in this country at that time. And I had my reward. Very seldom do I have praise in the house except
from my hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and my hon. friend the member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who are too generous to me.

speechtext: You deserve much more praise than you get.
