speechtext:
Thank you, sir. On
March 9, 1936, the Hon. Norman McL. Rogers, then minister of labour, an hon. gentleman who was so kind to me, said this, at page 994 of Hansard'.
May I say this, too: the hon. member for Temiscouata, by his industry and persistence a year ago. laid the foundation for the work we are seeking to carry on now in that direction.
He was speaking of collecting information on unemployment, and went on:
No one can question the desirability of securing this information at as early a date as possible; certainly no one who has any acquaintance with the problems confronting social service agencies in Canada can doubt the wisdom of obtaining and analysing this data. Already some of the returns have come in from the provinces. As soon as it is possible to summarize that information I propose to lay it before this house.
The Department of Labour had my report mimeographed so that it was available to all members of the house, to whom it was sent so that they would be familiar with that angle of the labour situation. That report was prepared by the member for Temiscouata with the aid of a stenographer, work which it was said it was impossible for the Department of Labour to do. There must have been something wrong with the department. But afterwards an unemployment commission was appointed, of which Mr. A. B. Purvis was chairman. He was a great friend of Mr. Dunning. The commission studied unemployment conditions in this country, but the only man who gained anything from all the work of that commission, which cost half a million dollars, was precisely Mr. Purvis himself. It served no other purpose. When the report was tabled I threw it on the floor to indicate that it was absolutely useless. It was a gesture of indignation at incompetency. Then I wrote a letter to the Minister of Labour. I had been working very hard to improve the conditions of labour and had done a work which had been praised, rightly or wrongly, by the minister of labour of that day. He told me that my work was the cornerstone of the unemployment policy of the government, Then everything was sabotaged by that commission. My letter was as follows:
Industrial Relations

Riviere du Loup, Que.,
August 13, 1939.
The Honourable Norman McL. Rogers,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Hear Mr. Rogers,-[DOT]
Because the figures prepared by the Purvis commission both on employment and unemployment were wholly unsatisfactory and useless, I offered you, two months before the prorogation of last session, to make within a month a classification of the unemployed according to their previous occupation.
You answered me that a new classification could be made by your departmental staff from the figures gathered by the Purvis commission and that it could be completed up to date by recent information supplementing that received by the Purvis commission.
On July 22 your private secretary forwarded me two shapeless compilations referring only to part of those who were unemployed eleven months before, in September 1937.
My first objection is that, in spite of what you told me, that compilation is out of date and therefore useless.

I wonder if it is the new flag we are to have. If I may go on now with the letter, I shall not have much to say about labour afterwards, because like everyone else I am very anxious to go home. To continue:
Even if those figures were up to date and referring to a month or two previous to the date of the issuance of the classification, they are equally useless for many reasons:
4.	Their disposition is absurd;
2.	There is no index with indication of pages;
3.	The occupations are too much detailed;
4.	The positions of similar trades are not put together;
5.	They are not summarized in general trades (a) by provinces and (b) by cities of the same province;
6.	There is no comparison between the total population and the total number of unemployed in provinces and cities;
7.	It is incomplete because it refers only to unemployed on relief in cities of over ten thousand population; etc., etc.
As the work done by your departmental staff is shapeless and useless, there is no room for it in my office and I return it to you by the same mail.
Let me add that it is a matter of -regret that very few of your departmental staff know how to work intelligently. I have understood at first that it was your intention to have that work(?) prepared by your departmental staff because they did not like someone outside your department to do that work properly or at least sensibly, in order that any one could understand something in the unemployment problem of to-day in this country.
With half a dozen worthy exceptions which I could name to you, the whole staff of your department^ from your deputy minister down, should be fired at once for the public good. It would be the first step for the relief of unemployment in Canada, and it should be so.
I have told you personally what I think of them and it is the truth. So long as you keep them in office instead of getting rid of them, there shall be no improvement in the unemployment relief policy.
I regret also not to have listened to my first thought and not to have done the work this year in spite of you as I did it successfully, some years ago, in spite of your predecessor in office, the Honourable Wesley Gordon.
Sincerely yours,
Jean-Frangois Pouliot.
May I now read the answer I received, and I may say that Mr. Rogers was a most tolerant man. He did not object to that criticism because he understood that it was offered in good will with a view to improving the conditions, which were very bad. I quote:
Ottawa, August 17, 1938.
Bear Mr. Pouliot:
I have received your letter of August 13, 1938, in which you refer particularly to the classification of the unemployed by the Regis-

Industrial Relations
tYation Branch of the Department of Labour. Your objections to the present method of classification will be brought to the attention of those charged with the work of registration.
From such information as I have before me, I cannot agree that your criticism is well founded. This however, is a matter of opinion.
I appreciated that at the time, andi told him so.
I have never objected to criticism from any source whatever and have always welcomed any suggestions which might improve the efficiency of the Department of Labour. I doubt, however, if any useful purpose is served by the general condemnation of officers of the department. It is your privilege to make this criticism and it is mine to disagree with it when it assumes the form of a general indictment. Nevertheless, I am ready at all times to discuss these matters with you as we have done in the past.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) Norman McL. Rogers.
This letter is to the honour of the late minister, and I have read it because I do not want to be interfered with in what I have to say regarding the Department of Labour. I will tel'l the minister-and hon. members know my views in this legard-that it is most unfortunate that the Department of Labour is controlled by the intelligentsia we have in the east block. The minister may deny that if he wishes, but the departments at the present time are not all under the supervision of the Prime Minister. They are under the supervision of the intellectuals of the east block, men from Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard and other places. They are intellectuals who are never in contact with the people, who have never been in contact with labour men, and it is they who make and dictate the policy of the Department of Labour and of other departments. These men, a partial list of whose names I had on December 10 last, are a curse to the country, and it is time to dispense with that intelligentsia, the same kind of intelligentsia that has caused the downfall of Russia.

And now, sir to show you the stupidity of some people, just at the beginning of the war, before the minister got in, an investigation was made by the departments of Agriculture, Fisheries, Mines, Transport and by the timber controller, MacMillan of British Columbia, and they decided what was the period of peak employment. I quote this, sir, to show the stupidity of these so-called experts. I cannot give it for all the provinces because I have not the time. I will give it for Ontario. It is divided into three heads-primary industry, secondary industry, period of peak employment, for Ontario alone, as I say. I have the 6.3260-325
other provinces, but time will not permit me to read them. Logging, December to March. That is false, because in the summer time pulpwood is cut and the bark is taken from it, but logging is done the year round. Sawmills May to September. That is untrue. Boatbuilding, from May to July. That is untrue. Refrigerators, April to June; mining, nonmetallic, July to November; transportation, shipping, May to November. Saw mills, boatbuilding and refrigerators are classed as secondary industries. Let us look at the secondary industries:	building construction
from June to November; that is untrue. Shipbuilding and repairs from May to June only; service, hotels and restaurants, July to September-no one eats in a hotel from September to July, apparently. Ice manufacturing, from June to September. Toys, September and October; toys are put in the same class as building construction and classified as a secondary industry. It is typical of the stupidity of these fellows. I shall not read all the material that I have at hand but would the house have any objection to my putting on Hansard an article entitled "Elliott Little was Right" which was written by myself and published in Le Saint Laurent on February 4, 1943?

The article follows:
On Selective Service
Elliott Little was Right By Jean-Frangois Pouliot ("Le Saint-Laurent," February 4, 1943)
"In or out of parliament, darkness, neglect, hallucination must contrive to cease in regard to it; true insight into it must be had."-Thomas Carlyle.
Laws reflect people. I realized this fact, finding in history the clearest and most faithful exemplification of law. The contrary is also true, because in order to have a just notion of present-day politics, one must stop to consider the deeds of legislators rather than their speeches, the arid phraseology of orders in council rather than the ambiguous sentences and the bombastic periods of parliamentary debates.
It is enough to glance over the statutes of war sessions to realize that parliament is called above all for the purpose of levying taxes destined to cover huge expenditures over which it has no longer any control. The pretext of war gave the government an opportunity to substitute itself for parliament in settling any question through orders in council passed by virtue of the War Measures Act and by stretching to a great extent the scope of this act. Therefore, it is not so much in parliamentary legislation as in orders in council that we can see the rolling and pitching of the federal ship in the storm through which we are struggling. According to the British parliamentary tradition which is still followed at Westminster, the government is a committee of the House of Commons. Here, the situation is reversed. It seems that

Industrial Relations

parliament, which is called only as a matter of form, is now merely, for the government a cumbersome constitutional institution.
Of the thirty thousand orders in council passed since the outset of the war, published in the Canada Gazette and piling up over six feet high-the height of a tall man-we will mention only a few, just enough to throw light on the capital and so much discussed issue of national selective service, in other words, of the conscription of labour.
When selective service, created by order in council in March, 1942, was announced in parliament, it had already taken effect three days before. Its purpose was to compel each person to contribute to the utmost to the war effort and, with this end in view, to maintain the balance required between the army on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the war industries as well as those which are essential for the upkeep of the army and the civilian population.
After the Mobilization Act of >1940 took effect, the conscripts were called to their military training by the registrar of the National War Service Commission, established under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National War Services, the first incumbent being, to our great surprise, the Minister of Agriculture. One can enlist only as a volunteer in the navy and the air force. That commission, which acted as a manning pool for the militia, was sending most of the conscripts to training camps. This was done with so little discrimination in Quebec that the members of the commission were successively replaced. They are responsible in a great measure for the shortage in man power which our region is now suffering in agriculture and forestry. Even before the adoption of selective service, we had to fight many battles for the recognition of its principle, and also to have agriculture, forestry and railroad industries considered as essential to the war effort.
It was under such circumstances that the Minister of Labour started with the adoption of order No. 5038, in June, 1942, enacting that it was essential to prescribe a greater use, by employers and employees, of public employment offices with a view to using our manpower most efficaciously in the war effort and reducing excessive shifting from one plhce to another.
Was the government feeling the ground ? After a six-week test period, the conclusion was reached that a drastic change was necessary in the method of calling conscripts. It was then decided to withdraw this task from the Department of National War Services and to transfer it to selective service under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. After providing for the establishment of secret priorities and for the stabilization of employment in the agricultural field, order No. 7595, dated August 28, 1942, prescribed a very simple procedure. In the case of employment in other fields, it was necessary to obtain permission from the selective service representative, with right of appeal, to the National War Service Commission. In other words, that commission was being turned into an appeal court, not against its own decisions, as was and still is the case, but against decisions rendered on first hearing by the local representative of selective service, in cases where the latter would have illegally refused, or unjustly revoked, an employment permit. The local representative of selective service would have .been kept constantly posted as to requisitions coming, not only from militia headquarters, but also from the essential industries, and he would have been in a position to assign {Mr. Pouliot.]
conscripts judiciously to the militia or industry, according to their aptitudes and experience, and taking into account requests on hand deemed reasonable, in order to maintain the necessary balance between militia and industry and preventing any shortage of essential manpower. That order in council, which was so sensible, was to take effect on September 1. It remained a dead letter, for the sole reason-or a sentimental order-that personnels of registrars' offices should not be reduced. This unbelievable explanation was publicly given in Quebec by an authorized person. Newspapers attest it.
So it was only to maintain, in spite of everything, some 300 employees, most of them useless-especially unmarried people without any military' record and some very young girls-in the registrars' offices of Quebec and Montreal that the government did not dare apply the very principle of selective service, which is of urgent necessity, and that the calling of conscripts -was not decentralized by being entrusted, as it should have been, to the numerous selective service offices. This is even less understandable as we hear nothing else but complaints about shortage of manpo-wer in the large war industries of Quebec and Montreal.

We do not know what happened behind the scenes, but by order in council No. 8343, dated September, 1942-748 others had been adopted in such a short interval-the regulations of 1940 applying to national war services were revised for the third time. Those who are mobilized and who do not answer their call may now be taken by force to camp instead of to prison-not to an essential industry-by order of a magistrate or of a justice of the peace. The National War Service Commission kept its initial functions and its first designation^ and remained for ten days only under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National War Services.
On September 26. 1942, the administration of regulations covering national war services was transferred by order in council No. 8800 to the Minister of Labour. The Department of National War Services had. therefore, lost all reasons for its existence: it had been laid bare and vacated just a few- days before the appointment of a new minister.
The fair distribution of our human capital between the militia and industry can be obtained only through a central organization having perfect freedom of action. Up to then, the national war service commissions had served only to fill the ranks of the militia. According to the provisions of the orders in council creating it, selective service was to insure not only the normal functioning, but also the gradual increase of industrial production. Mr. Little, its director, knew that very well. He keenly wanted the organization of which he was the head to serve industry as w'ell as the militia. Hence the indignation of jingoes and the campaign of the press accusing him of posing as a dictator and of trying to encroach upon the authority of his minister. There is an explanation for everything.
About that time. I heard out of sheer coincidence of the arrival incognito in Canada of a so-called expert, one Alexander Gunn, an official of the British government, whose services were supposedly to have been requested by the Canadian government to carry out the transfer of what he. Gunn, believed to be non-essential industries, to what he, Gunn, believed to be essential industries. No newspaper had mentioned the

Industrial Relations
comings and goings-over the whole country- of this newcomer. I gave the scoop of this news to the Ottawa Journal.
Here is a resume of this interview:	"In
Canada, as far as the government is concerned, the first qualification of an expert is not to be a Canadian. It is unbelievable that an outsider who does not know anything about Canada, about Canadians nor about their affairs, should be called to decide who, among our business men, will survive the storm. Is it impossible to find in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, to mention only our greatest centres, Canadians who are, not only as qualified but much more so, to initiate and carry out to a successful completion such a difficult and delicate task? Why such obstination in shrouding in silence his doings and even his name?" Seeing the intention to sabotage his work, Little, the Canadian, left. Gunn, the non-Canadian, remained.
By order No. 10,924, dated December 1, 1942, the regulations of national war services were revised for the fourth time under the designation of "regulations governing mobilization of national selective service." The old national war service commission survived all those amendments. Its duties are exactly the same to-day, with the same personnel intact, but under another minister. It is called now "The commission of mobilization." In order to give a just idea of the part it plays at present, we have learned from the best source that "selectitve service conforms to requests made by the Department of National Defence and that the registrars act accordingly." What is the result of so much zeal?
The newspapers reported, on January 27 last, that at the end of December, 1942, Canada counted 732,000 men under arms, that is, 33 per cent of the male population of Canada between 19 and 45 years old. It was said that
150,000	men would have been needed between March 20, 1941, and December 26, 1942, but that conscription brought up only 107,677. In a period of 21 months, conscription was responsible for only 1/7 of the men under arms. After such a poor result, why let the jingoes and junkers make so much noise with impunity and disorganize our industrial life?
We clearly demonstrated that the task of selective service should not be restricted to satisfying the demands of militia headquarters. We have the soldiers. They must be well armed, well equipped, well clothed, well fed and well cared for. The subsistence of our civilian population must be also assured. Besides, we imposed upon ourselves the obligation to provide our allies with arms, munitions and food supplies. If we want to keep up our speed, it is elementary and essential that our manpower be well distributed.

It is high time for action. All the provincial ministers of agriculture view the future with alarm. Did not the minister for Ontario declare in London, on January 13, that we are not far from food shortage, and did not the minister for British Columbia, on the same day, go as far as proposing to the Minister of Labour, at Victoria, to organize, for the defence if our territory, an army composed of women, in order to leave farmers and their sons on their farms where they accomplish essential work for our war effort?
Since the situation is so serious, we persist in maintaining that the policy set forth by the government in order No. 7595, dated August
63260-325J
28, 1942, was imposed by the needs of the moment, that no reason whatever existed not to apply it, and that this policy is the only rational means to offset the shortage of manpower.
That is why we beg the government to abolish immediately all the commissions called "mobilization commissions" and to assign the calling and distribution of conscripts to selective service offices, not only in Quebec and Montreal, but in all regional centres of the country.
Now that the government has deemed it opportune to publish the total set for, and reached by military conscription, have we not the right to ask for the same information in respect to manpower needed by and available for war industries and other industries essential to the war effort, for example, in the agriculture, forestry and railroad industries, to name only three of that category? We shall see, then whether Mr. Little was right in asking that the calling of conscripts be decentralized and that the care and responsibility of directing them to the kind of activities in which they can be most useful to the country, be left to local representatives of selective service.
Then I received a tip that a man by the name of Gunn had been lent by the British government to come here as an expert to organize the classifications of labour. I gave that tip to the Ottawa Journal. It was a scoop, and I expected other newspapers to publish it. I did not care to have my name attached to the news, but I wanted it spread from ocean to ocean to show the kind of secret work which was being done to sabotage labour. This expert by the name of Gunn came from London. He was the son of a-

Ottawa Journal, October 21, 1942:
Would limit big jobs here to Canadians Pouliot objects seeking executives outside
An appeal to the government is being made this week by Jean Francois Pouliot, M.P. for Temiseouata, to appoint experienced Canadians to important administrative war posts, instead of seeking executives outside the country.
"Here in Canada," Mr. Pouliot told the Journal to-day, "the first qualification for an expert in the eyes of the dominion government is that he shall not be a Canadian. As long as a man is an outsider, whether he has accomplished anything in his own country or not, he is at once rated as an encyclopedi a of general knowledge.
"A recent example of imported executives is the appointment of an Alexander Gunn, of London, England, who has been loaned by the British government to ours, to act as a special adviser to the director of national selective service.
"Mr. Gunn, I am informed, is here to supervise the transfer of what he finds non-essential Canadian industry to what he finds essential Canadian industry. I have nothing to say against Mr. Gunn-far from it.
"But it is incredible that an outsider without first-hand knowledge of Canada, Canadians and Canadian business, should be called in and asked to decide who amongst Canadians engaged in trade and commerce shall survive. Is it impossible to find in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto. Winnipeg and Vancouver, Canadians who are not only as well, but much better qualified to undertake such a complicated and delicate task?"
Mr. Pouliot stated that anyone who has studied the question of essential industry is well aware of differences between Canadian and British industry. In Britain, he said, many
[Mr. Pouliot.1
industries which Canada might regard as nonessential to the war effort are retained in production to maintain foreign trade and obtain necessary funds through foreign trade. The contrary might very well be true.
He felt strongly that Canadian executives who had built up powerful war industries from the ground and accomplished great things were those best qualified to analyse essential and non-essential industries.
"This question of ruling on essential and nonessential industries is one of vital importance", Mr. Pouliot said. "I cannot see how anyone but a Canadian could possibly be qualified to handle it. The British system could well be used as a guide to refer to, but problems arising are Canadian problems and must be handled by Canadian methods.
"I have made inquiries about the matter, and I am puzzled as to why Mr. Gunn's name has been hidden from the press and the public.
"There is a vast difference between the Canadian and the United States governments in this respect. When the United States required a man to do the same type of selection, it appointed Mr. Justice James Byrnes, a selfmade man thoroughly familiar with American business and American economic life, who resigned his seat on the United States Supreme Court to become stabilizer No. 1, and direct the greatest experiment in planned economy ever dreamed of in that country.
"I feel strongly that we in Canada should follow the example set by the United States in choice of an executive to reorient Canadian industry, and I implore our government to give this question their closest attention.
"I wish it to be understood that I am offering no criticism of our selective service officials in Canada. My dealings with Mr. Elliott Little, director, and Paul Goulet, associate-director, have always been most cordial and pleasant."
I shall tell you why I object so strongly to Gunn. It is because in the United States there was a revision of essential jobs by the wartime man-power commission. In Canada it was entirely different. There was no list of essential jobs. There was a numerous list of unessential occupations, and it was only with the approval of the minister that a man could be considered as fulfilling an important job.
When I come to it I must remind the house that General Tremblay, a gallant soldier who was one of the two or three inspectors general of the army in Canada during the war, became a minor clerk in the Department of Labour. He was lent by the Department of National Defence precisely to drag into the army as much as possible men who were engaged in essential occupations outside of the army. He was at selective service. I praised very highly Mr. Paul Goulet, the first time I mentioned him. With regard to selective service he is the right arm of the minister. He has done exceptionally well and deserves special praise. I admire General Tremblay personally, but one cannot approve his appointment as a minor clerk in the

Industrial Relations
Department of Labour, particularly when he was an inspector general in the army for quite a while.

He was not a brass hat there; he had no hat at all. He had a bare head. Soldiers suffered because of that. There were serious grievances and injustices to the soldiers, and wrongs which could have been redressed by the general if he had occupied his important office in the eastern command. He could not be found; he was under the wing of the Minister of Labour. I have special praise for the Minister of Labour because he was in favour of amnesty for farmers from the end of 1942 until the beginning of 1943. He was ready to grant amnesty to farmers and give them the opportunity to report without having any charge laid against them. The only man who objected to it was General LaFleche, because he thought it would be a handicap to him in being appointed to the cabinet afterwards. I know whereof I speak; I know my onions. I give credit to the Minister of Labour for what he intended to do in that connection. If that had been done there would have been no complaint in the country.
Another thing that I have done for the working classes is to prevent the imposition of conscription on women. I have a letter which I notice comes from the information services. It is dated 4/9/42. In this letter it states that Mrs. Rex Eaton, assistant director of selective service, is announcing a scheme of registration for women. It was for everybody. When we look at it we find that it states the inscription will permit the making of a complete inventory of all women who are ready to second men in the pursuit of war. It says that eventually all women will be inscribed in each category, but that they wish to proceed with care and method. If hon. members look at the Votes and Proceedings of March 18, 1946, they will find information about the inscription of women. There was only one inscription. All women of Canada were not registered. It was stopped because the policy was changed. Then I asked the following question:
On what date was it decided to discontinue such registration and for what reason?
The answer was as follows:
This was designed as a "spot" registration only. It was not planned on a current basis nor was any subsequent one or any in other age groups necessary.
Something occurred after the first registration. It was suspended for a time, and then the election in Charlevoix-Saguenay came
along and my hon. friend the sitting member (Mr. Dorion) ran as an independent. There were three other candidates. Had any one of the three other candidates been elected we would have had conscription of women, and I considered it my duty at the time to support the sitting member so that we would not have the conscription of women in this country. It was precisely the election of that hon. gentleman that cut short the idea of the government to establish the conscription of women in this country.
Moreover, sir, I can talk to labour men in any part of this country, because I have always fought for respect for the dignity of men in overalls. Throughout the war I considered that those who were working in all trades and occupations in essential industries were not slackers, that they were deserving of credit and that they ought to be respected. Labour does not forget that. But there is something else also. I was complaining about the intelligentsia that adorns the Department of Labour, and even the outside intelligentsia to which the department often has recourse. At the time of the tramways strike in Montreal I asked the Minister of Labour for some information, on March 31, 1943. I asked what was the news. The men engaged by that company were communicating with members of parliament asking for their assistance in settling the strike; and on March 31, 1943, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) was informed by the Minister of Labour that the strike was settled. On April 2, 1943, I read in the house a telegram I had received from Mr. Elphege Beaudoin, president of local 790 and president of the provincial federation of labour, asking us to offer our assistance to the strikers, and here in the house I asked the Minister of Labour if he would permit me to go to Montreal in a conciliatory mood to try and do something for those men. His answer was no, that Mr. Goldenberg was going there; and Mr. Goldenberg, who a few days before had settled the strike which was not settled, was sent there again and made a mess of it. It is always the same story. I see by the report that Mr. Brockington was named as conciliator. Mr. Brockington is a very fine man, but he is no better than any member of the committee who might have gone there to discuss the matter with the men. I have respect for my colleagues, and I prove it now. My contention is that the members of parliament should get rid of all the boards and all the intelligentsia and all the big brains, and should come together to settle the business of parliament and settle the business of this country without regard to party considerations. I appreciate the fact that all members of par-
Industrial Relations

liament do not put the political touch in their speeches, that even if they disagree, partisan political considerations are not to be found in what they have said,

I thank hon. members very warmly, and I thank you, Mr. Speaker; and I take this opportunity to express the affection I have for my colleagues. I am not perfect; nobody is, but I try to do my best, and they know that in my work here I am sincere. I shall remember their kindness of this moment together with the kind words which have been said to me by my colleagues from Broadview (Mr. Church) and Davenport (Mr. MacNicol).
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, with the background a member of parliament has in his fight to promote the interests of labour, there are things in this report with which I cannot agree, though naturally in the main I am for it because it is full of good will. However, I cannot agree to this reference to Mr. Brockington as mediator. I repeat that once it becomes necessary to designate a mediator, it seems to me there are enough members of the house who are competent and who are familiar with labour problems, who could meet those who have difficulties, so they may understand that parliament is the home of the people and that the spirit of parliament with regard to all individuals in this country is a fatherly spirit, a benevolent spirit; that the idea of parliament is not to exploit the credulity of the electorate at the time of an election. As soon as the election is over it is 
the duty of parliament to bring help to those throughout this country who are in distress, as far as that can be done.
With regard to the proposed provincial code, -I believe the settlement of labour difficulties should not be passed' over to the provinces. Even though the provinces have certain rights in regard to labour, the parliament of Canada should be supreme to assist workers in their endeavours to agree with their employers.
Finally there are the wartime prices and trade board and the regional and national war labour boards. We have a board here and a board there; they are the causes of difficulty. Mr. Gordon may be right, Mr. Gordon may be wrong, but he is not a member of parliament. My contention is that the decision should be made by the minister, over his signature. At the present time Mr. Gordon is under the Minister of Finance, and what he has decided affects the Department of Labour. All departments are entangled together; it is impossible to know with whom we have to deal. We go to this one, we go on to that one, we are sent from pillar to post, and all these men are irresponsible in the constitutional sense. We have difficulties with them; and if they are not erratic I cannot understand their ways of expressing their views and making their orders.

So far, Mr. Speaker, I think this discussion has been confined almost entirely to members of the house who were members of the committee. Not having been a member of the committee, perhaps I might discuss the matter from the point of view of a member of parliament who tried as best he could to follow the proceedings without actual attendance in the committee.
When this report was brought down I turned to it to see if what the house intended on July 16 had been carried out. Hon. members will remember that on July 16 the steel strike had occurred', and there was general alarm in this house lest production should be interfered with and serious results follow, with the further result that the house decided virtually unanimously, though at the time I said I thought the decision came too late, that the industrial relations committee should meet and go into the matter of industrial unrest throughout the country, particularly the matter of the steel strike. That seems, from the reading of the record, to have been the intention of the committee when it met;

Industrial Relations
for I find that, following the resolution to appoint a temporary chairman in the absence of the chairman, the first motion made was by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and read as follows:
Resolved, that consideration of the steel strike be the first order of business.
Apparently that was carried. Then, looking at the proceedings for the first full day's sitting of the committee, we find at page 45, on July 19, that the hon. member who first made the suggestion in the house that the industrial relations committee should be called together, namely the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), said this:
I am making this motion-
That was to call the various parties to the steel strike in.
-in order that we may get some speed in this task of ours towards the desired end of restoring that industry to production.
In reading this report I can find nowhere in it any direct reference to the dispute which occasioned the calling of the committee together, namely the steel strike.
In my opinion the report presented to the house by the committee represents a complete failure to do what the House of Commons hoped it might do. And because I think the committee failed so conclusively, apart from all other reasons, to do what the house expected it to do, I am going to oppose concurrence in the committee's report, in order to make my protest effective. After all, the only way in which one can make an effective protest in parliament, no matter if he may agree with some portions of a report, is, when the time comes, to register that protest by way of his vote in* the house. I intend to register my vote because of the failure of the committee to do the thing the house really intended it to do. I wish to say as well that I am opposing the report because of certain obscurities in it.

Perhaps it is the kind of report some people might have wished for. It is a report which is so indeterminate that it means very little either to the house or to the country. Certainly it is not the kind of report we had expected; nor do I believe it is the kind the country expected, in view of the situation across Canada at the present time. I believe the country expected the committee to produce a responsible formula or a set of proposals which would make possible the resumption of urgently needed production-not two months or three months hence, but immediately.
In this respect the report shows no sense of urgency, nor the slightest willingness to grapple with the real problem at stake. It may be said in retrospect-and I think it is true-that the appointment of the committee may actually have delayed settlement, and may have been detrimental to the resumption of production; for what it actually did was to buoy up hope on both sides that there would be a settlement, and to shelve the actual negotiations for four weeks or so, during the time the committee held its sittings. If that is the result, then I say that at this critical time it is something which at least we should deplore.
I followed the proceedings of the committee as carefully as I could-perhaps not as carefully as I might have done, had the business of the house not been as heavy as it was. It is unfortunate that the business of the house has been so heavy for the past few weeks, and that hon. members have perhaps not been able to read all the transcripts of evidence sent to their desks. But the major point, it seems to me, which emerged from the committee was that the government and its agencies had
Industrial Relations

become responsible for the situation that had occurred. It is their arbitrary and obstinate insistence upon placing a ten-cent maximum on the amount that may be permitted in a wage increase which has brought this about.
To me, this is a most deplorable situation, and for this reason, that the struggle becomes not a struggle between a union and a corporation but one between a union and the government. That, in itself, is a bad thing for any country in which it occurs.
I read the evidence regarding the ten-cent limit, and I could find in the record no scientific justification whatsoever for that limit. The most striking part of Mr. Gordon's evidence, and that of the Minister of Labour himself, was that they could not give a single scientific reason why ten cents had been chosen as a limit, and not fifteen cents.

speechtext: As a matter of fact I think everyone will agree that it is impossible to accept a limit of ten cents, or any other number of cents, that would apply to all industries fairly and justly. I will tell the minister what I think to be the only scientific way of arriving at a proper wage level. It is to take each industry, and sometimes each corporation separately, and to consider the relationship of wage costs to total costs-and, in addition to that, particularly in these days, the productivity per man. That has gone up considerably during the war, let us remember, on account of the improved machinery we now find in industry and, incidentally, particularly in the steel industry, where the furnace3 which have been installed and paid for are more efiicient than those used in Canada before the war.

ductivity of the individual in that industry should bear some relationship to the amount he receives in wages; in addition to the productivity per man, the profits of the industry, the reserves which have been built up by the industry, the working capital and other financial factors, and the relation of the particular industry to the economy as a whole, the standard of living and wages of the workers concerned, and all the factors- not one, but all the factors-which go into the making of price on the market. I readily admit that all these factors will vary from industry to industry and sometimes from plant to plant in the same industry. Therefore the attempt of the government to set an arbitrary over-all figure of ten cents for the entire industry or the entire wage level of all industries is, I think, unscientific, quite wrong, and provocative of unrest in the ranks of labour.
In to-day's newspapers is a Canadian Press dispatch which indicates the position that another labour minister in Canada is taking. I have in my hand a press dispatch appearing in to-day's Montreal Gazette, which states:
L^our Minister Pearson announced to-day the British Columbia regional war labour board \viJI approve applications now under consideration tor wage increases in excess of ten cents hourly and leave it up to the federal government to accept or reject the findings.

The action we are taking is done believing that many, if not all of the requested increases, are justifiable in all the circumstances and also because we believe that the wage situation must be clarified if we are going to maintain maximum production," he said.
Following what Mr. Pearson has said, a little thought will, I think, prove to this house that the most serious interference with production which we can have is because of labour unrest and strikes, and that the most serious danger of inflation is not a five-cent increase for the workers in one industry, but an interference with production. Indeed, interference with production may inflict upon our country a greater measure of inflation than almost anything else can do. The danger of inflation at the moment is due to a shortage of supplies, not only of steel, building materials and so on, but of many other articles. The great need both to avoid inflation and to serve the people of this country is to produce more and more. People now have money in their hands, the accumulated

savings of the war; those savings represent a demand, and the only answer to the demand is to supply goods and services so that we have plenty, and thus to interfere with the rise and avert the danger of inflation.

hand the small increase which the unions are asking is not to raise the standard of living of the workers but to maintain it at the level to which they have been able to bring it during the ivar and previously over a long period of struggle. subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I had intended to make a few remarks concerning the committee's report and particularly with regard to section 6 thereof. However, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has just made a statement, in which there are certain things I feel I should like to reply to very briefly. He suggests that wage costs should be tied to total costs of productivity, and he makes the suggestion, a very plausible one, that wages and profits should be related to each other.
Industrial Relations

On the broad humanitarian ground there is much reason to believe that that is a proper suggestion and one on which we can nearly all agree. But I would point out to the hon. gentleman the great difficulty in doing that in a scientific way. Let us assume -that these steel corporations, or some of them, have made large profits and could pay fifteen cents. Let us assume that for this year. Remember, however, that during the war these corporations have been operating at 100 per cent capacity and operating for immediate destruction. In many cases extra plant was built which is unlikely to be capable of use in the post-war era because of the simple fact that now we are producing not for destruction but for construction, and the goods that we shall produce, particularly in steel, will not be immediately destroyed, but will last a very considerable time. Therefore the absorptive capacity of the market, while it is great now, may not and probably will not be as great in the years to come. We must remember that this is not a business cycle and it is not the fault of capitalism. It is merely a phenomenon that happens after all wars. You manufacture for destruction and the entire product you manufacture is destroyed within a few hours, so that you have to manufacture again. Tanks and everything else made out of steel, shells, guns, are produced for destruction and naturally you need a tremendous capacity. But once the war is over, you begin to produce such things as motor cars and other manufactures of steel, which we hope will last for years instead of merely for a matter of hours. That is one of the fundamental economic transitions we have to put up with after emerging from a period of war.
It is easy to say, and it is an interesting and sympathetic thing to say, that wages should be tied to profits. I agree with it, but in a period of transition I doubt whether there is any firm that can tell what will be their profits during the next few years.
I wish to say something more in this regard. In the automobile strike in the United States, the fact-finding committees that were set up by President Truman worked very well and assiduously for upwards of a year, and from the last report I have had they were unable to determine upon a formula which would tie wages to profits. This was one of the things the industrial relations committee discussed, and we discussed it quite seriously, -both in open and in closed meetings. We found-and the evidence is there-that it was difficult or almost impossible to arrive at any formula which would, in the present transitional period,

tie in wages to profits, no matter how desirable that was. I merely want to show the difficulty of arriving at these wage rates and differentials, and I would quote one paragraph from an article by Professor Lloyd G. Reynolds, who is director of the labour-management centre at Yale university. He has this to say on the subject as quoted in the American Economic Review.
The individual firm is caught between the area and the industry. Conditions within the area, particularly the wage levels of other firms, determine the minimum which it must pay. The wage rates of other firms in the industry, ceteris paribus, will determine the maximum which it can afford to pay. If the latter figure is less than the former, the firm will in time be forced out of operation; but if it is greater the firm can be guided by the wage level either of the industry or the area. Developments in the industry may lead the firm to make wage changes independently of any developments in the local labour market. Indeed, for firms in competitive industries which are geographically dispersed, it appears that the industry is normally the dynamic influence in bringing about wage changes, while the influence of the local labour market is merely passive or permissive.
I put that on record to show how extremely complicated this business of tieing wages to profit really is. While we have every sympathy with doing that, it is something on which one cannot put a yardstick and easily evolve a formula. There is one thing with which I should like to agree and quite forcefully, namely, the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that at the present time inflation is caused more from the almost complete paralysis which is going on in the country, caused more by the lack of productivity than by anything else. To-day we are really in serious danger of inflation, not because of any wage scale or any differential, but for the simple reason that we are not producing. Something has been said about the pressure of money. Despite the fact that money is decreasing in the hands of the workers and that their security is decreasing, which is a tragic thing, the volume of money to-day i3 creating tremendous pressure on the whole price structure. The lack of production is . becoming more serious every day that the strike continues.
I wish to say a few words about the recommendations in the committee's report. I should like to touch briefly on the labour code. It has been obvious for years that a labour code is necessary in Canada for two reasons. The first is the fact that our manufacturers are young and have expanded more quickly than the industries and the manufacturers of any other land in the world. Our tremendous increase in manufacturing potential has been the marvel of the rest of the world; but with this tremendously rapid increase there have

Industrial Relations
been certain growing pains. With old-established industries management was able to grow up with labour. In Canada we have had such a rapid increase that in many cases management has not had time or has not been able to understand the problems of labour. Over and over again that was brought out in the evidence of the committee. Management has been primarily interested in the production, selling and dispersal of the goods it produced. Consequently in many industries labour relations have been almost nonexistent. We did not have time; we grew so rapidly. The same can be said of many unions. The industrial union in Canada has been a growth of the last few years. Consequently in many cases it did not have the seasoned counsel of unions elsewhere. With these two problems, one from the management point of view and the other from the union's point of view, it was inevitable that there would be a clash and we are having it now in one of the most critical periods of our history.
During the war I spent some time in the coal mines in Great Britain and I was privileged to sit in at a labour-management committee of one of these mines. I have never seen more genuine interest expressed by anybody than I saw in the problem of production at that mine. I came back and I saw conditions in one of our coal mines.-Instead of cooperation, instead of ability to see each other's point of view, I saw nothing but bitterness and the petty meannesses that two sides in any dispute can wreak on each other. Therefore, when we talk of labour-management we have a great distance to go along that line. Unless we can arrive at some way in which, labour and1 management can and will sit down together, we are sure to have continued trouble throughout Canada. Therefore, when the suggestion of a labour code is made by this committee-and it is their first recommendation-I look upon it as probably the most important single piece of projected legislation that this country has to create.
I wish to deal now with the machinery that is already in existence. We have seen a great number of strikes and industrial disputes, many of them caused and brought about unnecessarily, brought about because the two parties to the disputes were unable or unwilling to ge.t together. There were innumerable meetings and conferences; hours and hours were spent by the two sides in endeavouring to come to some sort of compromise; in some cases months were spent. After you spend hours and hours and even, months in talking, the human being becomes a little bit desperate. Many times action, and perhaps unwarranted
action, has been taken because of the despair or I might even say the frustration felt by the two parties in their endeavour to get together. So that there must be, and the committee recommended, an acceleration and simplification of the processes of settling labour-management disputes. We cannot afford to take months and months for any plant to come to an agreement with its workers.
The next point I want to make is this. We have seen in this committee, and it has been admitted by the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, that there has been virtually no liaison between his board and the war labour board. That is an intolerable position. The chairman of the price control board says it is his opinion that an increase in basic wages above a certain limit will put very strong pressure on the whole price structure of this country and that he will not be responsible for continuing price control if greater increases are permitted1; yet his representatives have not been sitting in with the people who are trying to evolve a formula for the settlement of these difficulties, either on a single plant basis or on a multiple plant basis. In view of that situation I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that there is a very great lack in our whole wage and price structure, and in my opinion this has done a great deal to cause the tragedy of industrial strikes we see across Canada to-day.
I come now to a problem which is somewhat sinister. It was apparent that in 1944 there was an organized agreement between certain unions to make a concentrated drive. Those plans were furthered at the conference in Quebec, I think, in 1945; and the result is now apparent in the industrial paralysis we see about us. It would be easy, yet it would be wrong, to say this was organized by the communist party. To say that certainly would be untrue. But it would be equally untrue to say that the communist party has not had a hand in causing a great deal of the present unrest. I say that to-day Russia is like an African snake called the Ringhals Cobra. This peculiar snake, has the power to spray and spit venom great distances, and wherever this venom lands it produces a festering sore. If it lands in your eye it blinds you. Well, Mr. Speaker, there are certainly places in Canada to-day where there are festering sores, and there are certainly places where parts of the population are blinded. That cannot be overlooked in any discussion of industrial unrest in Canada to-day. I want to quote just one sentence from a speech delivered quite recently by Mr. Churchill. He was speaking of England, but it is equally true of Canada. He said:
Industrial Relations

Even here in our patient community soviet propaganda has been steadily making headway backwards. I would have not believed it possible that in a single year the soviets would have been able to do themselves so much harm and to chill so many friendships in the Englishspeaking world.
I say that with a certain amount of sorrow, because I was the first member of this house to advocate the recognition of Soviet Russia by Canada.
I now come to discuss, in a little detail section 6 of the report. I have been interested to notice where the objection to this section comes from. If I may say so, it comes from the extreme right and the extreme left. Basically this section was inserted in the report for the simple and democratic purpose of giving those who were going to be affected by a strike an opportunity to say whether or not they wanted to strike. It is as simple as that. We have a number of strikes in Canada, very serious strikes, too, by unions which have not been certified in the industry. We have plants which have been strike-bound literally for months, the strike being called by a union where no certification vote of any kind has been taken. I have evidence that at a number of these plants the strike action was not popular and was not wanted by the employees. Surely the men who are going to be affected by a strike should have an opportunity of saying whether or not they want to strike. Surely that is the basis of our whole democratic system. Surely that is the basis of everything that we have believed in connection with the rights of man. Surely, then, the individual must have the right to say whether or not he wishes to take strike action. And he must have that right safeguarded, not by an organization that is prejudiced one way or another, but by an unprejudiced organization such as the Department of Labour. I say that is one of the fundamental things in labour relations in Canada to-day.
I have information given me concerning the General Electric strike in Toronto. I have not verified this information, but it has been given to me by sources which I consider reliable. There were three strike votes taken at three different plants. One strike vote was taken in the union hall, and the vote was ninety-two per cent in favour of striking. The second strike vote was taken by union management, and the vote was eighty-six per cent to strike. In the third vote I understand the ballots were counted by the parish priest, or somebody else equally trusted by the employees, and the result was sixty per cent against taking strike action.
Those plants were all similarly situated, and were all doing more or less the same type of

work. These figures which I have given clearly signify that in one plant, where an independent vote was taken, a considerable majority voted to maintain production, whereas in the other two plants under union auspices the votes were overwhelmingly to take strike action.
That, Mr. Speaker, is more than coincidence. I have letters and affidavits in great numbers from people in my riding who are employees of the Anaconda American Brass Company, stating that the decision to strike was certainly not a majority decision of the employees in that plant. The plant has been out since April and has caused untold harm not only to the men who have been forced to take strike action but to the entire building industry in Canada. It is the only brass plant in Canada producing certain types of tubing. Every house being built needs the product of that one company, and, as I say, it has been out since April. If that strike action was taken without a majority of the employees in the plant wanting to take that action, I say it is undemocratic, wholly wrong, and wholly against those principles which we try to live up to, and which we profess.
I would say one thing more concerning the vexed question of law and order, and in this I speak only for my own riding. That law was flagrantly broken is beyond any peradven-ture of doubt. Prosecutions have been taken, and convictions have been registered as a result of the breaking of not only the criminal code, the common law, but also the laws controlling picketing and the use of force. That cannot be tolerated by any government in Canada-and when I refer to any government I refer to any municipal, provincial or federal government.
We cannot allow the law to be broken, and say, "Well, it is de facto; why worry about de jure?" Let the thing continue like that, and we shall have business going from bad to worse. And, if I may say so, that is the policy publicly advocated by the communist party in Canada. I do not say the people who took this action were communists, but I do say that is the policy laid down publicly on platforms when members of the Labour Progressive or communist party speak in Canada.
I wish to reiterate once more why I believe that clause 6 may be the turning point against strikes which might be described, as wildi-cat strikes, even though in many instances the unions have been recognized. I am in entire agreement with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he says that it is fundamental that before one takes action or before action is taken in his name as a member of a union and an employee of a plant, before action is taken

Industrial Relations
which will affect his entire economic life and security, he must have an opportunity to say whether or not he agrees with that action.
But I say I believe that the insertion of clause 6, imperfectly worded as it may be, may offer the individual employee the freedom to express his views and wishes secretly and fearlessly, and on his decision strike action will be taken. If the committee has done that, if we have brought that measure of freedom to the individual worker, it may be that this will have been the corner-stone of a labour charter for Canada, for which we all devoutly hope.

Section 1 is a pious hope for a future sinless industry. It will not do any harm. It proposes that, we have a dominion-provincial conference. long time to integrate their ideas to the point where they will get together. No harm in it, but no immediate good.
It is also suggested "that matters coming before the regional and national war labour boards be handled expeditiously." Well, who does not want every important matter handled expeditiously? Nobody could vote against a sentiment of that kind, so obviously I supported it. There is no harm in it, but certainly no immediate good is likely to come from it.
In section 3 the committee recommends "that a measure of union security should follow certification." What measure? So far the committee's report has not been interpreted in detail by any responsible member of the government, so I am wondering what, and how big, the measure is. If it is the same kind of measure I have in view I agree with it. It is ambiguous. If, however, it means what I have in view it means quite a lot. I would say that "a measure of union security" should be as large a measure as company security.
We come to section 4: "Law being the basis of our society, your committee condemns" so and so. Mr. Speaker, that is a platitude which has been reiterated, I suppose, as many times as there are people old enough to know what law and order mean.

I said, constantly reiterating that we believe in the observance of law is a platitude. We all believe in law. Everybody in a civilized country believes in law and order. Everybody who comes to this parliament, I assume, believes in law and order. Burglars and thieves and murderers believe in law and order if they are going to be subject to summary lynching by the gang who catches them and if law and order will give them some protection for the time being. Everybody believes in law and order; so that is not a helpful or concrete or very wise decision for a committee to hold over forty meetings to arrive at. However, I agree with it; there is no quarrel so far as that is concerned.
Section 5 is a recommendation "that the law of picketing be studied with a view to its modernization and clarification" and so on. I think there is no disagreement there at all; I believe that is a very proper recommendation. I suppose that practices grow up around
Industrial Relations

any organization as it is building, which require revision from time to time to bring them into conformity with our conceptions of law and order. Therefore I can support it.
As to section 7, I am not so sure what it means, but it says:
Your committee recommends that the controllers appointed by order in council P.C. 2901 be instructed to implement the terms of such order with such modifications as the government may determine.
That in itself is one of the reasons I would have liked the minister to make a statement, to interpret some of these things.
Some people in reading P.C. 2901 may concentrate on paragraph 9. That paragraph states:
It shall be the duty of every person in the employ of any of the said companies at or in any authorized establishments of the companies to perform the duties of his employment until the authority of the controller is revoked; and every person who fails to perform his duties as aforesaid as herein required without lawful excuse, the onus of proof of which is upon him, is guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to a fine of $20 for each day or part of a day on which he fails so to perform his duties.
I am sure that some people in this country when they read that will wonder whether, without a statement from the minister, without an interpretation of section 7 of the committee's report, every striker in Stelco and in other plants, under controller Kilbourn, who is to-day on strike is to be subject to a fine of S20 a day or whatever other penalty may be involved in the section.
I come now to section 6, about which there has been so much debate and controversy. I do not know that I need deal with it for any length of time. I know that if it means what it says it does not mean what some hon. members here interpret it to mean, and if there is any statement in or section of this report which should have been clarified by a competent official of the government as soon as the report was tabled, this is the one. The minister was there when the controversy took place. Only three of us on the committee voted against that. Their names were mentioned the other day: the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and myself. I voted against it particularly on the grounds that it did not mean what those who were promoting it said it meant, and that it should have been clarified and put into the kind of words which would show exactly what it meant, if it does not mean what it said.
