subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
A moment ago I was dealing with section 6 of the committee's report and the minister said: Why didn't I say these things in the committee, meaning in the camera sittings where the matter came up? To answer the minister I had to refer to what happened in camera. The minister said on the floor of the committee that he would make a statement in the house and he has not made it. Other members have referred in the house to what was said during the camera sittings of the committee; so why does the minister single me out as one who should not break that apparently very breakable rule when it does not embarrass anybody to have it done? However, I will leave the minister out unless he insists on interfering.
Let me read section 6 of the committee's recommendations:
Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may, at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision, to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
If it is good to have that in there, and assuming that it means what it says or means what some have said it means, why not have another section reading: Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may, at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a vote of the shareholders of the company, without proxy, be taken to determine the wishes of the shareholders regarding the requests of the union for increases or improvement of working conditions.
One is just as fair as the other. I do not think one would be any more acceptable to labour than the other one will be. It would not be acceptable to the kind of organizations I know something about. But it would not be an illogical corollary to section 6 as it stands at the present time. I remember that when Mr. Hilton was on the stand he questioned the right of the union leaders to call a strike and demanded that the question be referred back to the workers. When the hon. member for Cape Breton South asked him if he would agree to have the company's position referred back to the shareholders Mr. Hilton was astounded and would not even consider that that was a reasonable proposition. He was engaged by the shareholders to do the job and his word was law. But when a couple of thousand workers engage a man like Charlie Millard to do.their job, Mr. Hilton expects him, every time he runs into a place where he must use his own judgment and
make his own decisions, to run back to the workers to find out if they support Charlie Millard or Mr. Hilton. Why it should be right in the one case and wrong in the other, I cannot understand. I see no difference between the two positions.
I now come to a section that I am possibly even more concerned about in some respects. I refer to section 2, to which my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred. I am going to refer to it in more detail. Section 2 reads:
Your committee is convinced that continued price control is only possible with a reasonable measure of wage control.
There again is ambiguity, because "reasonable" can me.an so much or so little to anybody. If you are arguing with your wife and appear to be getting the best of the argument, what happens? She says: Now, be reasonable. On the other hand, if she is getting the best of it, you say: Be reasonable. What is "reasonable" except somebody's point of view of what will suit them best? So that when you put into a recommendation a statement like that it does not carry a great deal of weight.
But section 2 as it stands carries more weight I think than the actual wording would suggest to the casual reader. I say that for this reason. To me, section 2 is a clear acceptance by the committee of the government's rigid determination that while wages for workers and prices for farm products must be controlled in the interests of price control, interference with the profit position, now or potentially, of companies is an interference that will not be tolerated. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), in addressing the house last night, spent a good deal of time in telling of the efforts of Mr. Donald Gordon to convince the committee that ten cents was the over-all limit. As has been said before, and I agree, Mr. Gordon offered no concrete factual evidence that ten cents was the correct figure. It may be nine and a half cents; it may be three cents; it may be thirty-three cents. But he simply said ten cents and made a long statement in support of it, supported by no facts whatsoever. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply tried to tell us in his speech last night that Mr, Gordon probably did not prove his point; but nevertheless, because of the position he holds, his advice should be heeded. We have had too many cases in this country, Mr. Speaker, of ordinary everyday people who have been placed by fortuitous circumstances in positions of great responsibility before whom we were supposed to bow the knee with adulation for every single utterance they make. We
Industrial Relations

certainly have had a liberal education in the last four years designed to make us worship Donald Gordon and accept every single statement he makes. But it is a matter of opinion whether he is right. Mr. Donald Gordon's statements may be correct. I do not believe they are correct. I differ with Donald Gordon as to the increase and1 I will give my reasons. When price fixing first came into effect the idea of price control was to maintain the existing relationship between costs and prices and profits. It was the base from which he worked. This position was maintained pretty generally during the war, even though government subsidies were extensively used to maintain it. The maintenance of margins of profit, together with the vastly increased war business, netted great profit positions for many industries, and now they are loath to relinquish that wonderfully favourable and privileged position they occupy. I absolutely believe, from the statement placed before the committee, which is on record, and from my own experience, that the steel companies are quite able to pay the full amount of the union demands. It is indicated in the statements themselves.
I know there is controversy. I know people will say it cannot be done. They will pick little figures out of big books and prove this and that by them, because there is an old saying with regard to figures and' people of certain classes, and we are none of us free from it. We like to prove our point. But I will draw on my experience in considering the reasons why I do not believe that Donald Gordon is right, no matter whether he believes it or not.
First, he based his position on the belief that you can maintain the spread of profit over and above all costs, including wages, that the industries are used to having, and more if they can get it, and they will be the sole judges as to how much profit must be made, having no responsibility whatsoever to the public in the operation of the business of making that profit. I am going to go into something I know as much about as anyone in this house, from which to draw my experience. I have spoken about these matters before for different reasons, and, therefore, when I mention cooperative associations I am not going to go back to a debate that we have closed. I am going to debate this question from the point of view of the experience of cooperative organizations I know about, and compare them with other industries of a similar nature which are not cooperative and which I also know something about, because I worked for them.

I am going to take, first, the matter of cooperative elevators, or pool elevators if you want that name. That is their actual name- Saskatchewan pool elevators. Twenty-four years ago, twenty-three years ago, and up until twenty-one years ago, you could not have a bushel of grain handled on the street in a country elevator for less than seven cents a bushel for commercial grades and six cents a bushel for contract grades. In that year, we, a bunch of farmers, got together and put our own money into the building of an elevator system. Why? Because we knew that seven cents and six cents was too high a handling charge and that the profits to the company were too great.
We had no factual information. No private company would give us their statement, but a few men like myself who had worked for some of these companies were able to give a general idea and to create the belief, which was a conviction, that profits were too great. So we took the only way we could to prove it. We built a system of our own, and to-day we have reduced handling charges in years of big volume to as low as one.cent a bushel, and for the last four years, for not more than three cents a bushel on the street, in the car, rolling, or any way you like to have it, right down to spot position at the head of the lakes.
I am not saying that in order to show how brilliant we were, because we knew we were only ordinary mortal human beings, and if we were able to engage management to operate our elevator system and clear us of all costs of operation at those reduced handling charges, then other men in the grain trade could do the same. It has been proven that these other companies, because of the competition we afforded, have had to reduce their handling charges to the same figure as our own; and they are still in business.
Does the house expect me to want any greater proof that companies can do their business at less profit, or, on the other hand, can pay more of their earnings in wages, without affecting the price of the goods or the services created by those industries? As a matter of fact, while reducing those handling charges we improved the actual service given in the country elevator. When we were paying the high handling charges we also lost all dockage that was in our grain, because the company who bought our grain owned it and frequently there is a good market for the dockage in wheat or in any other commercial grains when they go to the terminals and are cleaned, because many times there is good wild oats, buckwheat seed and other foreign

Industrial Relations
matter which is good for feed or feed mixtures, and whoever sells that, when there is a market for it, makes good money.
So that not only did we reduce these handling charges but we paid back to ourselves the value of the dockage in the grain after cleaning it out, with the result that the farmer who happened to have more dockage, in consequence of ' a bad year for weeds, received some recompense for the dockage in his grain. Other companies have to do the same thing when there is anything in it, and they are still in business.
At one time the spread between what is called straight grade grain and damp grain was as high as thirty cents a bushel, nearly always as high as twenty cents, and in those days if a farmer shipped a carload of No. 1 northern wheat which graded damp and went through the drj'er at the head of the lakes, it came out of the dryer automatically numbered 3, two grades down, because the private companies would not spend money on research or put in a proper drying equipment so that the grain could be dried without bringing about that chemical process which caused it to lose its grade. When we went into business we put in proper dryers. To-day the spread between straight and damp is seven cents a bushel, and other companies are in business. You can put No. 1 northern damp grain in a dryer, and it will come out No. 1 northern and cost only seven cents a bushel because of drying it. The companies are in business now, and therefore they could have done this before and made profits.
I have tried to prove in that statement, not what we are doing in the west to reduce the cost of handling grain, but that companies can do with less profit and should do with less profit, and their income should be spread out more in one or both of two directions, or a combination of them; that is to say, higher wages to the people working for them or a lower price to the people who buy their commodity, or a position half way between these two, but not in more profit to the organization that does the job.
I can give another example. It is not so long ago-far less time than the grain business I have been talking about-back in 1933 and 1934 when we were establishing our cooperative refinery in Regina, that we were told by competent and highly placed officials in the major private oil companies that it cost up to S+ cents a gallon to manufacture a gallon of gasoline out of crude oil. We did not believe it. We could not prove it but we had the conviction that it was not true. So we set up our own refinery and have cut in two
the cost of manufacturing gasoline, and other companies have done the same and are still in business.
If they could not afford to do this, how are they still in business when they have to do it? Of course they can; and Stelco, Dosco, Algoma, Westinghouse and the rest of them, I fully and earnestly believe, can do the same. I am inclined to believe, as was suggested this afternoon, that on the part of somebody in the scheme of things there is a stubborn determination that bossdom is going to maintain its role, no matter who gets hurt, the public or the country. I am afraid that Donald Gordon, wittingly or otherwise and possibly this government unwittingly, or both together, are helping to maintain that uneconomic and unfair position. The returns for industrial production are to be set by the owners of industry; the workers will get what the boss wants to pay them; the consumers will pay what the boss wants to charge them, and the remainder will be profit for the companies. Again that is important to our people in the west.
In this debate we have not heard very much from the west, and that is why I had the temerity to take part in it. We are getting squeezed in this process. We have gone through the war years doing our little patriotic best with worn-out machinery to produce whatever was required in the largest volume possible. We have bought victory bonds to the best of our ability. I started with the first victory loan campaign and finished up with the ninth. I have a beautifully engraved and decorated memento from Mr. Magee, chairman of the provincial war finance committee, showing my part in the campaigns. It was not greater than anybody else's. I am giving it only to show that we have done our little bit; it was not great; it was not outstanding; it was just our little best. We were always ready to obey Donald Gordon and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe); to obey the request of the government to do everything we could to help our position in war production; to play our part in the hope that, when the war was over, we would get some relief in the form of machinery which we required and the other things that were needed; along with price adjustments for our products. Over a year after the end of the war we are still waiting. I am continually getting letters from men out in my section of the country. This morning I received one from a man with 800 acres of wheat. He lost his crop last year. He has no combine to harvest his crop this year and will lose it if we happen to run into bad weather. That is an indication of the hard-
Industrial Relations

ships through which these people are going and which they hoped they would not have to experience at this time, particularly when the war is over.
If the government continues to pursue its policy of maintaining the private system, the private position of Stelco at Hamilton and others, regardless of whether the workers are being properly treated or not, and if production is to be curtailed in a basic industry we of the west will face another year and possibly two, when we shall not have the proper machines to prepare our land, put in our crop for the coming year and take off the crop in the fall, if we are fortunate enough to get one, a crop which hon. members and everyone else in the country together with peoples all over the world need so badly. It is important to us; but do not think for one moment, if hon. members should have that idea, that you are ever going to sell the farmers of the west the old idea, which used to prevail that labour is all to blame. Some hon. members said that the press always puts the blame on labour. I agree with that. Since I have been in the House of Commons and the disputes started, I have not yet read a headline in one of the Ottawa papers or in one of those so-called capitalist or private enterprise papers which ever gave a fair break to labour in a dispute. No; we do not find them giving the labour side of the picture. No matter how they try in radio talks or in speeches made in the house, they are not going to make the farmers of the west believe that their enemies are labouring people. The farmer knows who made a profit when he was getting low prices for his products. He knows who makes the profit when he buys his binder, his combine or his plough. Compared with the profit to the one who sells it, it is a good many to one. It is the worker who makes the plough, the reaper and the other farm machinery, and who has the family who is buying the farmer's butter, eggs and oatmeal. We believe that the farmer's market is much more important than profits to a few industrial owners who can only eat so much, wear so much wool and live in so many houses at a time. The farmer wants labour to get a fair share of the national income at the present time.
If the recommendations which came out of this committee, and if what appears to be the government programme, is to be the continuing programme of the government, then I am afraid-no, I am not afraid, I am sure there will be tremendous repercussions not only around the plant where the difficulty is taking place but all across the country, because the farmers believe the workers, the producers and the consumers should have a prior claim over (Mr. Bentley.]
the productive power of industry in Canada before anyone is paid a profit over and above what is commensurate with the responsibilities of the job he has to do.
I would make this suggestion, and I shall be chastized for this, Mr. Speaker, so, as other people sometimes do, I shall admit my error before I say it. I should have thought of this in the committee but I did not think fast enough. On one occasion the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) told me that I did not have a legal training. I frankly admit that. I do not know whether I am sorry for it or not. I have had some other kinds of training which have stood me in good stead in times of trouble. I have depended largely on fast footwork and other things to get me out of trouble, and have not had to learn much about legal matters. Had I had a legal training, I might have suggested this, but other members of the committee have legal training and either they did not think along the same lines as I did or they forgot it. Had I thought of it, I would have made this recommendation. Section 2 of the report reads as follows:
Your committee is convinced that continued price control is only possible with a reasonable measure of wage control.
What is a reasonable measure of wage control? It really does not mean anything to a legal man or anyone else. It means "reasonable" to the people who are using the phrase at the time. I say the section should read in this way, and had I thought of it, I would have so recommended. I am sorry I did not think of it in the committee. The section should be reworded to read this way:
Your committee is convinced that continued wage control is only possible with positive price control.

speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the debate, this afternoon. Many things have been said with which I can agree. Some things have been said which I had intended to say, but I shall not take up the time of the house to repeat what has already been mentioned in the debate. I think I can safely say that the country as a whole, and labour, will be disappointed with this report. The country as a whole was expecting that the report would deal with some definite solution, particularly of the steel strike. I am sure that labour in the country will be dissatisfied with the ambiguous language and general terms of the report. In that connection I wish to read a section of the statement of the wage coordinating committee of the Canadian Congress of Labour on this matter. Referring to the report of the committee on industrial relations, the Canadian Congress of Labour wage committee said:
Not only has the house committee failed to do anything to settle current strikes but it has for a period of four weeks created the illusion and the impression in the minds of the public, management and workers that the members of the house committee were going to settle the strikes.
I think that is a correct statement, Mr. Speaker, and I believe you will find it to be the general attitude of labour throughout the country.
Before proceeding very briefly to deal with some sections of this report, I wish to say that some hon. members have expressed the opinion that strikes in Canada are largely due to communist activity. Several hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party have made that statement. I believe these hon. gentlemen completely misunderstand the fundamental reasons for the discontent which exists among the great masses of the Canadian people. In the first place, I would say the reason for this discontent is that we have fought a bitter and difficult war, during which the people were told they should look forward to a period of peace which would inaugurate a new social order. The people of this country are expecting that new social order. Then I would say the second reason for the mass discontent which exists to-day is the desire for economic security, the desire to maintain and improve the standard of living. When hon. members blame communist activity for the discontent that is in the country I think they entirely misjudge the situation. I am a farmer. It may seem strange that two farmers in succession should speak on a labour question. I have had experience with labour
organizations only during the last five or six years, but in my experience I have found that the great mass of the people are reasonable, willing to compromise, ready in many cases to accept less than they should. But I am quite sure that at the present time there are large numbers of Canadian workers who are thoroughly dissatisfied and who have solid reasons for being dissatisfied.
Before dealing with one or two sections of the report, I wish to say that I was disappointed because the report did not contain some concrete recommendation in regard to settling this steel strike. In this respect I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and others who have spoken to the effect that the committee should have recommended the last proposals of the steel workers, which I think were very fair and realistic proposals, which were advanced with full knowledge of the situation, and which were modifications of the original proposals. I believe the committee should have recommended those proposals first to the controller, then to Mr. Brockington as the person who was to negotiate between the employers and the union, and, if that failed, I believe the committee should have recommended those proposals in its report to this house.
I am not going to go through the report, but I do want to deal with one or two sections. First, I should like to refer to section 3, which reads:
Your committee recommends that a measure of union security should follow certification.
I think that is an unsatisfactory and ambiguous statement. As a matter of fact it means little. I think-and in this respect I agree with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll)-that following the experience of the last few months with the Rand formula as it is operating in the Ford plant, the committee would have been well advised to recommend the Rand formula in this report. If only that concrete proposal had been contained in the report this committee would have recommended to parliament something worth while.
The other section with which I wish to deal briefly is section 6, which reads:
Your committee recommends that the Minister of Labour may, at the request of either party to an industrial dispute, and if he deems fit, either before or after a strike is in progress, direct that a strike vote be taken under government supervision, to determine the wishes of the men affected as to whether a strike will take place or otherwise.
I want to express my hearty disapproval of that section. On casual reading it does not sound very serious or dangerous, but it con-

I shall make myself
clearer in a moment, and shall explain more fully what I have in mind. It may be said in fairness that the minister has certainly a tough assignment on his hands. I have known him a long time and I am convinced of his sincerity. But through him the government has reaped and is reaping severe criticism. The statement is often made on the street that the whole situation has got out of hand. Perhaps we may better judge the truth of that statement after the minister has reviewed what he has attempted to do; perhaps he can vindicate his position. I shall be interested to hear what he has to say in that connection.
I do not intend to deal with the several sections of the report, because that would be repetitious. It has been referred to by other hon. members who have spoken. Not only because I sat on the committee, but because of my contacts for a long time, I am convinced that the formation of labour groups, with collective bargaining, is the right of labour, so long as they do not attempt to take the law into their own hands. I believe that is conceded.
It is also apparent to all that price and wage coordination is a necessity. This is recognized by most people who are interested in the present difficulties. I believe, too, it is
an established fact that practically all labour groups attempt to be fair in their demands. At least that has been my experience respecting those with which I have come in contact. I think that was borne out largely in the deliberations of the industrial relations committee. Likewise I must say from experience that I believe it is becoming more generally conceded week after week that most employers have the interests of their employees at heart and are learning to get closer to them. That is gratifying to me. I believe many others hold the same opinion. There are those of extreme views on both sides who may not agree with what I have said, but by and large that will be found to be the general opinion.
If the industrial relations committee has done nothing else it has focused attention on the methods which have been employed recently, largely by certain individuals, to stifle production. That may be a strong statement but I fear it is true. An early meeting of federal and provincial labour heads is urgently needed. The minister has indicated to the committee that he proposes at an early day to try to bring that into effect.
I am convinced that a national labour code in Canada is essential. If there be objections to it, I think it is about time that those objections should be aired, and let us find out what they are, and if there is some remedy which can be applied. The public must be informed on this issue also, so that we may try to coordinate the interests of labour and management across this country in an endeavour to find a pattern to avoid disputes of this kind.
I now turn more particularly to the present situation at Hamilton. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that there is a situation obtaining there which must be rectified. Either the controller is being what is commonly called "hamstrung" by somebody to whom he is answerable, or he is certainly not rising to the occasion and meeting his responsibilities. As the hon. member has said, if that is the case, and no satisfactory explanation is forthcoming, it is about time that a change was made there. The minister should make the position in that respect very clear. Perhaps this is one of the reasons why certain labour heads, in appearing before the committee, impressed upon us that they have a lost faith in the present government and the policies it has followed, more particularly in recent months.
Much has been said about the secret ballot. I have taken the trouble to discuss this with, not one or two, but dozens of men whom I consider to be the most sane and capable
Industrial Relations

members of unions, men who have worked for industrial institutions as long as twenty years and more. I have gained much knowledge from those men; they have often discussed this matter with me. Let me say here to some of the labour heads that there is much criticism among their own ranks of the way the so-called secret ballot is conducted. Some of the best union men go so far as to charge that there has been manipulation in many cases when a strike vote is called or about to be called. That is an important point, and it has a considerable bearing on the conclusions which I have reached in the present issue. I suggest that, if labour heads desire to retain public confidence, coercion of their members will never promote their cause.
Much has been said about the influence of communism in certain labour groups. Let me say to all right-thinking members of any labour union or any other group that the type of individual whom they entrust with their leadership will in large measure gain or destroy public confidence. Of that I am convinced. If public confidence is once destroyed the cause of labour can never regain proper recognition. There is an old adage that anyone can lead a horse to water but nobody can make him drink. That adage applies in the present situation to both management and labour.

speechtext:
I can hardly finish in that time.
As I said, the influence of communism is being felt in many places. Where there is attempted coercion there is an apparent danger; to try to force either management or labour to do something which they feel they cannot do is merely provocative. I was deeply impressed by some of the remarks of the labour heads who appeared before the committee. In most of their presentations I found a great deal with which I could agree. I want, however, to refer particularly to a few things that I find I cannot agree with and with respect to which I still await answers to questions which I asked in committee. I am still at a loss to understand why there is so much insistence that the three steel plants now on strike must be considered as one unit. I am unable to find any explanation of that. I think the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) covered the point and I shall not repeat what he said in that connection, but I am largely in agreement with

what he said on that subject. I am still convinced that much confusion and, I think, some damage have been caused by the insistence of labour that the three steel companies be considered as one unit because the interests of these companies are so diversified, their sources of raw material are so different and their costs of operation vary widely. I think those charged with the responsibility of calling the strike should reconsider that point.
I am also at a loss to understand why so many labour groups contend that every time there is a rise of one or two points in the cost of living there must be a corresponding increase in wages. It is my opinion-and I think this is borne out by what many others have said-that production will be the controlling factor or at least have very much to do with the cost of living in this country. I am optimistic enough to believe that if our production can be brought to the highest possible peak our worries about the cost of living will not be so apparent. So I ask the labour groups why it is that they are so insistent upon wage increases when, if production is only allowed to reach its peak in Canada, it will have a great deal to do with the cost of living in this country. If labour gets a five-cent increase every time there is a five-point rise in the cost of living, will labour be ready to take a corresponding decrease in wages in a business recession?
Talk to the man on the street, men earning their living in many different vocations, and you will find that they are puzzled over the insistence of labour on this point-for-point increase, an increase in wages always to accompany an increase in the cost of living, because the clerk in a store and the average wage-earner receives no such consideration. I think there should be a little more give and take amongst labour in that respect. I pointed that out in the committee and I still believe I am right.
I am also at a loss to understand why the 40-hour week was ever injected into this dispute at this time. In my opinion that demand was ill conceived. It was only last January that an attempt was made by law in the province of Ontario to regulate the hours of labour and bring about more uniformity by adopting the 48-hour wreek. But the ink was hardly dry on that law before certain labour groups across this country were demanding a 40-hour week. That is not reasonable. We must try out these changes. I say to labour groups that I think their demand for the 40-hour week was ill conceived. I may be wrong and I am open to be convinced, but that is my opinion.

Questions
Let me say to employers that they must observe the 48-hour week which is now the law in Ontario. They must give it a trial so that labour may get the benefit of it.
On motion of Mr. Lockhart, the debate was adjourned.

That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, to provide
(a)	that the chairman shall be eligible to become a contributor and entitled to benefits under any established pension fund of the corporation;
